utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. The 1st of March, 2011. Good morning to the accused, to Mr. Pusic, who is still absent because he's ill, but he's being represented by his lawyers, his counsel. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I am going to give the floor to the Prosecution for their rebuttal. utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, everyone else in and around the courtroom. May it please the Court, I will have some rebuttal that I think will take about 45 minutes or so, and then I'll be followed by my colleague Mr. Scott, and we have prepared a PowerPoint presentation that we'll be referring to during the course of my comments this morning. Mr. President, Your Honours, as indicated by Mr. Scott last week, among the issues that we wanted to address in rebuttal were response or rebuttal in respect of some of the legal points made by counsel during their closing submissions, and most of what I'm going to be referring to relates to positions advanced or remarks made by my learned friend, Ms. Alaburic, and also Mr. Kovacic on the issue of occupied territory. The first -- the first subject would be some remarks related to the question of the status of the Muslim prisoners that were held in HVO detention facilities, and this is dealt with more specifically on page 52550 of the transcript, and those are the transcript references that will be found. That's the location where the Trial Chamber will see the transcript references throughout my remarks. Defence claim that able-bodied men are not considered civilians unless proven otherwise. And just to sort of recap, the Prosecution position is that able-bodied men who are not combatants under Article IV of the Third Geneva Convention or under Article 43 of the Additional Protocol are indeed civilians. If they are not combatants within the definitions found in those provisions, then the Prosecution position is that those able-bodied men are indeed civilians. We refer the Trial Chamber to the remarks of the Trial Chamber in the Celebici judgement, which is useful to bear in mind that: "The fact that an individual is a male and of military age should not necessarily [justify detention]." Having said that, imprisonment of able-bodied men for security reasons requires an individual assessment, an individual assessment of the risk of that prisoner joining the enemy forces. And again, the citations and the support for that position are set out on the slide. Having said all that, Prosecution agrees that in respect of these proceedings, the burden is on the Prosecution to prove civilian status of the prisoners. We -- Ms. Alaburic made that assertion, and the Prosecution accepts that. However, the Prosecution does not accept the position that there is some default position for Muslim men of military age that makes them something other than civilians simply by virtue of the fact that they were Muslim men of military age. On our next slide I continue with this point. This is again referring to a position set out by Ms. Alaburic that based on the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army consists of active and reserve forces. Reservists are those subject to conscription. All able-bodied men are subject to conscription under BH law, and therefore, according to Defence, all able-bodied men are reservists or "noncombatant members of the armed forces." Prosecution response to that, Mr. President, is, first, we invite the Trial Chamber to really consider what the Defence are asserting here. What they're claiming is that there are no able-bodied male civilians in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's really what they're claiming, and that is not supported either factually or under international humanitarian law. Under the law, reservists, that is, those who have undergone military training and have reintegrated into civilian life, those reservists are civilians until such time as they are mobilised or called to active service. We provide the Trial Chamber with support for that position. The article by Mr. Melzer with ICRC. Thirdly, counsel referred to a status that they believe applies to these Muslim men of military age calling them as reservists, "noncombatant members of the armed forces." They are not members of the armed forces if they have reintegrated into civilian life or, indeed, if they are merely subject to conscription because they reached a certain age. The status of noncombatant members of the armed forces does exist, but it applies to armed -- to members of armed forces who have no combat mission, like judges, chaplains, medical personnel. Those people, if captured, have POW status or the equivalent of POW status, but that status itself, something called noncombatant members of the armed forces, does not apply to Muslim men of military age who were not members of the armed forces. Continuing with this, Mr. President, the Prosecution position is that therefore the "interned" able-bodied Muslim men who were not in active service of the armed forces were not "noncombatant members of the armed forces" under international humanitarian law. They were civilians, and when they were arrested and detained, they retained their civilian status. On this it's useful to note, perhaps counsel should have recalled or consulted with their client General Petkovic on his position regarding the status of persons who are not involved in active combat activities. The Trial Chamber will recall the testimony of General Praljak. This is at page 50785 of the transcript where he said that -- I'm sorry, Petkovic, General Petkovic. He was asked: "General if a member of the HVO, for instance, who was on leave, on furlough, rapes a Muslim woman, for example, is that a crime linked to combat?" And General Petkovic's response was: "No, that is not a crime linked to combat, because during that time he was a free civilian until he is recalled to join the army again." So to the extent General Petkovic appears to be saying that someone who was at one time a member of the armed forces and who has left the armed forces and has reintegrated into civilian life, that person remains a civilian, and if that is what he was asserting in his testimony here, that was correct, but the position advanced by my learned friend, with all due respect to her, is incorrect. One final comment on prisoner status. The Prosecution in its brief, as you know, Your Honours, has advanced the position that Muslim men who had been members of the HVO, who were arrested in the days following the 30th of June, 1993, we do not take the position that they are civilians. We have taken the position that they are entitled to the protection found under Article 75 of Additional Protocol I, which applies to persons whose custody -- who do not benefit from better status or better treatment under other parts of the Geneva Conventions. In her closing submissions, counsel for General Petkovic asserted that Article 75, Additional Protocol I is in the civilian population section or chapter of that Additional Protocol and it therefore only applies to civilians. Prosecution's response is that is incorrect. We invite the Trial Chamber to read the text of Article 72 of Additional Protocol I, which provides that that section, that chapter, is in addition to Rules concerning protection of civilians and civilian objects. It applies "as well as to other applicable rules of international law relating to the protection of fundamental human rights during international armed conflict," and the French text of those provisions is certainly in accordance with that, indicating that Article -- that the section in which Article 75 is found applies not only to civilians but as well as to other provisions in international law. In addition, the commentary to Additional Protocol 75 makes it clear that Article 75 applies -- or may apply to persons who are not civilians, such as mercenaries, for example, or, most importantly, to "other persons who have been denied prisoner of war status." So it's our submission, Mr. President, Your Honours, that Article 75 of Additional Protocol I does indeed apply to the Muslim men who had been members of the HVO even if they're not civilians. I'd like to move on now and make some remarks regarding what we call the duty to protect prisoners. It's a related point coming not only from international humanitarian law but closer to home here, the appeals judgement in the Mrksic case. The Defence claim that the Mrksic duty only applies to agents of the detaining power who find themselves with custody of prisoners of war, not every agent of the state, but only those who had that responsibility as they were effectively custodians of the POWs. Mr. President, the first remark or comment that the Prosecution would offer here is that although the Mrksic case is -- itself was limited in its facts to prisoners who were indeed prisoners of war, the rationale and the underpinning for the Mrksic holding as found throughout international humanitarian law makes clear that the Mrksic duty would apply not only to prisoners of war but to other prisoners falling into other categories as well, such as civilians or even Muslim men who had been members of the HVO who might fall within Article 75 of the Additional Protocol or even under Common Article 3. Prosecution position is that responsibility for the protection of detainees depends on the functions that that person carries out. Responsibility may lie based on domestic legislation, or a person may be responsible and have a duty to protect prisoners based upon his or her de facto responsibility based on custody and/or control over prisoners. So there's a de jure and a de facto, in our submission. De jure under domestic law, de facto based on custody, control, as the facts show. On this point, for example, one could say that -- and the Prosecution does say that under the domestic legislation Mr. Coric and the military police, as part of the Defence Department, had primary responsibility, custody and control of prisoners. We cite a couple of exhibits there, one of which is the instructions issued by Mr. Boban, which vested responsibility with the military police for providing internal security at HVO military prisons and also securing prisoners of war. That's an example of domestic legislation, in our view, that would assign responsibility for prisoners to Mr. Coric, the military police, and, since it's a part of the Defence Department, the Defence Department itself. Mr. Pusic, despite assertions made by his counsel during closing submissions, acquired de jure responsibility for prisoners in connection with his appointment as head of the Department of Exchange and also his appointment to the Stojic commission, which was formed to look into prisoners and the conditions during the latter part of the summer of 1993. On Mr. Pusic, Mr. President, just a slight digression. I'd like to take the Chamber to P07411. Mr. Pusic, at 52755, and at 52760, and really throughout the entirety of his closing submissions, asserts that he had no real authority. He was a small cog. He had no discretion. He was merely forwarding lists and that he didn't have the ability or authority to decide who could be released and that he played no real substantive role. Page 4 of this document, which is a report that he made on the work of the Service for the Exchange of Prisoners and Other Persons, that is his service, gives a good overview of the kinds of activities that he sat at the top of as the head of the service. Item 5 here, on page 4: "The work of the Service staff was mainly concerned with detained Muslims. As the status of prisons ... has still not be regulated," they put all the prisoners together in co-operation with ODPR, SIS, crime investigations department of the Military Police Administration. "... it also effected release from prisoners if detainees had complete documentation," letters of guarantee, transit visa, certificate, et cetera. "In this way, 304 persons were released ..." What this shows is that the Prosecution doesn't assert that Mr. Pusic had supreme or exclusive authority over prisoners. He and his service and his competencies were linked to others, other bodies such as those indicated here, and he played a substantial role in issues involving prisoner custody and release. He doesn't have to have played an exclusive role, and it's certainly not our position that he did so. The fact that he played a role that complemented others, that co-ordinated with others, certainly does not absolve him of responsibility. And more to the point, here, when we're talking about this duty, he certainly is among those having de jure and de facto control over prisoners, and he has a duty to protect them. One aside on this point. There were many repeated assertions concerning the credibility of Witness E made both by the Pusic Defence as well as Mr. Coric's Defence. What we see here is explicit reference by Mr. Pusic to a programme that is linked to the testimony of Witness E and clearly establishes that this programme on letters of guarantee and release linked to that was in existence and was an official part of HVO policy bringing together the various bodies indicated here, military police; ODPR, which is a bodily linked to president of the government, Mr. Prlic; SIS; Military Police Administration. Another document linked to Mr. Pusic in response to his assertions, P07124. It's a meeting of a working group held on the 11th of December, 1993. It was chaired by Colonel Biskic who had come in. By that point he was acting as an assistant minister of defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. He testified in this trial. And this is a very useful document again for dealing with or considering the role that Mr. Pusic played in matters involving prisoner treatment, custody, policy. Page 3 of this, Mr. Pusic takes the floor, informing those present about the various detention centres. According to him, the wardens of each prison, of each detention centre can provide the exact number of detainees being held, as well as the number of those being used to work. He said, and I'm moving up now, he didn't have a precise figure on prisoners because they were being constantly "taken away to work, mostly on preparation of the front line. On the next page, Mr. Pusic continues to present figures related to the numbers of prisoners in the various detention facilities. 1200 at Gabela. Mr. Bozic is present there, talks about the 2.000 who are being held at the Heliodrom. Moving down, this is a significant point on prisoner status. Colonel Biskic added to this that they especially needed the number of detainees who were members of the Muslim armed forces. Mr. Pusic said there were only five such cases. The next page: Mr. Pusic believes they should all be released but that at the same time all measures of organisation, protection, and security should be taken, and in particular, preparing the detainees so they can be sent abroad. And then finally, toward the end of the document, on page 10, Mr. Pusic believes that people over 50 years of age should be sent or, rather, handed over to the Muslim side, on the left bank of the Neretva. So here in December of 1993, we see Mr. Pusic taking the floor at a high-level meeting regarding prisoners and what the prisoner policy should be. He's expressing his own views. Basically, the younger ones who were in the detention facilities should be sent abroad. The older ones should be sent to the east side. Coming back to the slide, point number 3. The Prosecution rejects, and I mentioned this already, the Coric and Pusic Defence arguments that they've made repeatedly that because others may have had custody, control, may have had the ability to exert authority over prisoners, that they had none. It's our submission that responsibility does not require exclusive control or custody. The evidence shows that several individuals and bodies did have custody and control over prisoners in different spheres. It's our assertion that the duty to protect prisoners applies to all of them. Generals Petkovic and Praljak had custody and control over prisoners when prisoners were in custody of HVO units performing forced labour. Petkovic and Praljak exercised control over prisoners when issuing orders and approvals on use of prisoners for forced labour and granting access to prisoners and prison camps. The Trial Chamber will also recall that General Petkovic was personally involved in the negotiations near Sovici/Doljani and Jablanica, related to the Muslim prisoners who were being held there at the Sovici school. Next slide. Defence assert the international humanitarian law does not regulate the issue of competence, that is, who's responsible in a de jure capacity for prisoners. It is left to each individual country to decide who was responsible to deal with prisoners of war. Prosecution agrees with that submission. However, that's on the de jure side. De jure responsibility as assigned by domestic law does not preclude or rule out the existence, additionally, of de facto responsibility based on one's having custody and/or control over prisoners. Ms. Alaburic, in her closing submissions, asserted that the Prosecution did not plead that any legislative enactment or superior order delegated the duty to protect detainees to the Chief of the Main Staff. Here we identify those parts of the indictment related to allegations of responsibility concerning General Petkovic and prisoners. The indictment alleges he "controlled, collected, facilitated, assisted," et cetera. The Trial Chamber can see what's alleged. The Defence seeks to avoid responsibility based on Petkovic's de facto custody and control over prisoners. Even if he wasn't specifically designated under the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the law of Herceg-Bosna to be responsible for prisoners, that doesn't rule out, obviously, his responsibility for prisoners over whom he, in fact, exercises custody or control. Next Defence claim is that there's no evidence that any legislative enactment or superior order delegated the duty to protect detainees to General Petkovic. That is not correct. We refer the Trial Chamber to P05104. It's the order from Mr. Boban dated the 15th of September, 1993. I made reference to this in my closing submissions on General Praljak. We have that one. We can take a very quick look at it. Items 3, pointing out that: "If there are detention centres where not all conditions required ... are ensured, they should be immediately ensured and prisoners of war must be treated in accordance with" international law. This is issued to the Defence Department and the Main Staff. Item 7: "The HVO Main Staff shall inform all subordinated commands and units of this order and provide professional help in its implementation." Mr. President, Your Honours, it is the Prosecution position that this is an express delegation from Mr. Boban to the Main Staff that applied to General Petkovic who was the deputy commander of the Main Staff, as well as to General Praljak, who at that time was its commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Tomic wants to speak. You will have your rejoinder. I don't know. There may have been a massive mistake that would justify you taking the floor now, but you're supposed to do it later, not now. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. It's a technical matter. The Prosecution got instruction by the Trial Chamber that it should refer to new matters, but what they have been talking about was dealt with in the final brief of the Coric Defence, and I do not see what it is exactly in the Prosecutor's submissions that is supposed to be new. So that the Trial Chamber's decision is not being honoured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, normally your rebuttal should focus on what was said during the closing arguments of the Defence. Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I believe, Mr. President, that's what I've been doing. We are talking specifically -- rebuttal's obviously most closely linked to legal assertions made by counsel, but to the extent that we are using this to address assertions made by other parties, I think that it's appropriate to do so. It's clear that all Defence have made assertions and that we're attempting to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President, if I may be heard for a second. This is the problem. That's a confusion between rebuttal, such as to cross-examination, and rebuttal to closing argument. Now, if I was in the United States, this would be a great rebuttal, but we don't have that system here. The Tribunal here has made it very, very clear that rebuttal is only if there is a surprise, something that wasn't expected. None of this is a surprise. There was briefs and then there was argument. Nothing came out of the argument that should have been a surprise to the Prosecution, nor have they made that claim. That's why, in my humble submission, this is not proper rebuttal under the jurisprudence of the ICTY, and it's an abuse of the process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps if I may now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. This is exactly the kind of argument that I wanted to avoid. It would have been best if Mr. Stringer used his 45 minutes, and then if the OTP had used its three hours, and then after this rebuttal, you could have taken the floor on the Defence side and say Mr. Stringer made a mistake and the Chamber could draw its conclusions, because we're wasting time right now. We're wasting time. Let me consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber is asking the OTP only to mention the topics which were added in the oral submissions, during the closing arguments, and not to come back to what had been written in the closing briefs. What we're interested in is what was added during the oral submissions, during the closing arguments. And you must also, of course, always refer us to the paragraphs and tell us, as you said, on the transcript, counsel such said such and such and I don't agree with this or that or we're going to have this kind of problems cropping up over and over again. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you look at the slide it says Defence claim here number 4. That's an assertion that counsel for General Petkovic made during her closing submissions. It's a new assertion. They say that there is no evidence of any legislative enactment delegating responsibility for the prisons to General Petkovic. I've just shown the Trial Chamber the Boban order which in our view does make that express delegation. So I'm responding directly to a point that was -- was raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we will see this in due time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's -- let's move to the next slide. I'm going to skip a couple, because I'm starting to run over already. So I want to go to point 5. Again, this is raised by Ms. Alaburic. There's no evidence that the Chief of the Main Staff, Petkovic, exercised control over any detention facility. The Prosecution response is that this is irrelevant. The question is whether General Petkovic exercised control over prisoners and whether he or his subordinates had prisoners in their custody. That's the relevant question in our respectful submission. And we also submit the answer to that question is yes, he did have control over prisoners. Next item. The Prosecution, according to the Defence, did not plead that Petkovic found himself with de facto custody over prisoners of war or other detainees. Here we again referred the Trial Chamber to these parts of the indictment where specific allegations in the indictment are pled regarding his de facto custody and control over prisoners. We also assert or allege in the indictment that he was responsible for ensuring proper treatment of prisoners under international humanitarian law. Next point. The Defence allege there is no evidence that Petkovic had de facto custody over prisoners. In the Prosecution's view, that is incorrect. It's our position that Petkovic and Praljak did have custody and control over prisoners when they were in the custody of HVO units performing forced labour. And as I've said, when General Petkovic or Praljak issued an order relating to access to prisoners, use of prisoners for forced labour, et cetera, they were exerting control over prisoners. And of course, when prisoners were in -- on front line positions under -- performing forced labour, they were in the custody of the HVO. Finally on this point, counsel asserted that even if the Mrksic duty applied in this case, it does not apply to Petkovic, and the citation or the reference to that is -- is found there in the transcript. Again it's -- the Prosecution obviously relies on everything we've said so far on this, but in addition, the Trial Chamber needs to consider these things: In handing over prisoners to the military police, what did Petkovic and Praljak do to ensure and satisfy themselves that prisoners arrested and imprisoned and held in the custody of the military police would be protected, because we know from Mrksic that when prisoners are handed over to another body, the person doing the handing over has to ensure they'll be treated properly. We know that Petkovic knew and Praljak knew that the military police had engaged themselves in crimes repeatedly in the past. We know from May 1993, when they arrested hundreds in Mostar and put them in the Heliodrom, that they couldn't take care of them. They couldn't feed them. They had to turn to the international humanitarian organisations for help in that. So that certainly put them on notice that they were going to have a much bigger problem come early July when they started arresting the thousands. We also know that they knew, Prosecution asserts, that prisoners were being used for forced labour under a programme that was very extensively administered by the military police. So knowing all that, what did Generals Petkovic and Praljak do to ensure that the prisoners would be treated properly? We submit, nothing. Secondly, with while the prisoners were in custody, as we've said, Praljak and Petkovic were in custody and control to the extent that they issued orders on access, forced labour, et cetera. So again, Mrksic applies because of that. Thirdly, during my closing submissions on General Praljak, we went through the sequence of events by which the world became aware of the conditions, for example, at Dretelj when the prisoners were being released and the various media reports, the activities and the pressure put on the HVO to shut down the camps. We know that upon learning of all this, Praljak and Petkovic had a duty to take them back, to step in and ensure that proper conditions were provided. And the citations for that are here on this slide under Geneva III, also Geneva IV, on taking effective measures to correct the situation. Praljak knew, Petkovic knew, in our view, and did nothing. And as a result, that's another aspect of the Mrksic duty that does indeed apply to them. Next slide. This position is actually echoed in the expert report of General Pringle. Paragraph 77 of his report where he talks about the obligation to take prisoners back into their authority when they learn that the prisoners are not being treated in accordance with international humanitarian law. Finally on this point, Mr. President, as I've alluded to item C there on the slide, there is extensive evidence of the disclosures, media reports, international condemnation of the conditions and treatment in the camps. It was all very well known, and clearly, the Prosecution submits that Generals Petkovic and Praljak were aware of that. So again, having that notice, the Mrksic duty under international law imposes on them the obligation to step in, to assert their authority and to ensure that prisoners are being treated correctly if they're not being treated correctly by the military police to whom they had turned over the prisoners. I've got a last few remarks to make concerning Defence positions and assertions related to occupation and the duties that flow from being the commanding general of occupied territory. Mr. President, Your Honours, consider the Defence position on this. The Defence position is that the commander of the HVO may exercise such control throughout the territory as imposing -- as imprisoning all Muslim men of military age, but at the same time, the Defence asserts that the commander of the HVO bears no responsibility for the protection of women, children, and elderly who remain behind, living on their own throughout these same territories. If ever there was a case justifying application of the doctrine of occupied territory to hold a military commander responsible for failing to protect civilians, this is such a case. Not only were Petkovic and Praljak commanding generals over occupied territory when the law is applied to the facts of this case, but, in fact, each of them played a personal role in creating the very conditions that permitted the widespread crimes committed against Muslims in places like Prozor, Sovici/Doljani, West Mostar, Ljubuski, Stolac, Capljina. The first Defence assertion on this relates to notice. The Defence assert that they received insufficient notice or that the indictment does not sufficiently plead this as an issue in the case. Prosecution respectfully disagrees. We would first of all direct the Trial Chamber to the Mrksic appeal judgement, the paragraphs indicated there, 136 to 144. Now, Mrksic was considering whether the Defence had sufficient notice that they were charged with the Mrksic duty. So it's a different duty that they were considering, but certainly the Prosecution would submit the same rationale applies. And the rationale is that in considering whether there was sufficient notice and pleading, the Trial Chamber should consider the indictment as a whole in concluding or determining whether Defence had notice of their need to defend a duty such as the prisoner duty in Mrksic or, as we say in this case, the duty flowing from the commanding general of occupied territory. In our indictment, we've indicated or listed a number of the provisions there that relate to these issues. I'm not going to read them all to the Trial Chamber. It's worth noting in particular there are repeated references to duties, aiding and abetting, responsibility for failing to carry out duties, omitting duties, and there are two references in paragraph 232 to there having been not only an international armed conflict but also a partial state of occupation. Much of this is repeated or elaborated on in the Prosecution pre-trial brief, which is indicated there. Points on "territorial expansion," again Croat control, taking control of municipalities, securing municipalities. So in our view, again, all of these issues are sufficient and put the Defence on notice that these issues concerning control of occupied territory, as referred to in paragraph 232, would play a role in this case and form a basis for liability. The Trial Chamber will recall that it's not the first Trial Chamber to consider whether there was a territory that's occupied in this Tribunal. It was an issue that was dealt with in the Blaskic case, in fact, but more close to -- closer to home, Sovici/Doljani was expressly found by the Trial Chamber in the Naletilic-Martinovic case to be occupied territory. And of course, that same crime base, that same location forms a part of this case. So it's not clear how the Defence can argue that they didn't know that occupied territory would be a factor or an issue. The difference, of course, is that in this trial we have the commanding general here. We didn't have the commanding general here during the Naletelic trial. We invite the Trial Chamber to consider the extensive trial evidence related to issues of control, takeover, all of which, of course, bear on the issue of proving that the HVO had supplanted the lawful authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and was, in fact, in a position to exert its own control and authority over these areas, which is the standard as set out in our brief for finding the territories occupied. Finally, the Trial Chamber may recall the map that General Praljak presented toward the end of his evidence. He was cross-examined on that by me, and he was asked very direct questions about his role, responsibility for protecting civilians in the blue areas that were under the control of the HVO on the map he presented. I believe the Trial Chamber will recall the debate on that, but certainly it was a hot issue during his cross-examination. A second point raised by the Defence with respect to occupied territory is the claim that the occupation must be by foreign forces. The Defence appeared to be claiming that occupation requires the sort of classic belligerent occupation that we saw in World War II, for example. That is not the case. And just to state our position here, because Mr. Kovacic in his closing submissions stated that the Prosecution has not even indicated who the occupying power is, it's our position that it's the Croatia HVO side of the conflict. That's the same occupying power that was held to be in control of Sovici/Doljani in the Naletilic case. The Croatia HVO side of the conflict, an international armed conflict taking place on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Certainly Blaskic and Naletilic themselves stand for the proposition that you need not have a classic belligerent occupation or that Croatian armed forces themselves must be the sole or exclusive occupying power. Naletilic was the very same factual situation we have here. That is, Croatia exerting overall control over the HVO, while at the same time the HVO having supplanted the lawful authorities and in a position to and indeed exerting its authority and control over the occupied territory. In terms of further support for the view that you don't have to have a foreign or an exclusively foreign occupation, we direct the Trial Chamber to Article 47 of Geneva Convention IV, and this and a couple of the authorities that we're going to rely on that follow make it clear that, certainly in the post-World War II era, there was recognition that occupying forces would attempt to evade or avoid the responsibilities, the responsibilities that flow when territory does become occupied, and that Article 47 here is a response to that in attempting to recognise some of the situations that can arise and be employed in order to avoid the obligations that flow from occupation. Under the commentary here, you'll note, this is the first paragraph of the commentary, which says that: "During World War II, whole populations were excluded from the application of the laws governing occupation and were thus denied the safeguards provided by those laws ..." And then moving down to the second paragraph of item number 2 there. It's worth noting, because it's a situation that is very closely linked, in our view, to this case. "Of course, the Occupying Power usually tried to give some colour of legality and independence to the new organisations, which were formed in the majority of cases with the co-operation of certain elements among the population of the occupied country, but it was obvious ... they were in fact always subservient to the will of the Occupying Power." So we would respectfully direct the Trial Chamber to Article 47 of the IV Geneva Convention and the commentary as standing for the proposition that the classic exclusively foreign occupation is not required in today's world for there to be an occupation. In our book of authorities that we've submitted with our final submissions, we have included among those an excerpt from a much more exhaustive treatment of "The International Law of Occupation" by Mr. Benvenisti, and here on page 5, again, he echos this view that occupation can exist even when the occupying power exists through surrogates and other administrations, and even when it seeks to avoid its responsibilities under the law of occupation. "Today, however, such practice is the rare exception," he's talking about a declaration of occupation by the occupying power, "the exception rather than the rule. Modern occupants came to prefer, from a variety of reasons, not to establish such a direct administration. Instead, they would purport to annex or establish puppet states or government, make use of existing structures of government, or simply refrain from establishing any form of administration." And he goes on to talk about how they would not "acknowledge the applicability of the law of occupation to their own or their surrogates' activities ..." So in our submission, Your Honours, this is reflective of the law of occupation as it is -- as it exists in our world today where we have states, powers, in occupation, even though they may be acting through surrogates. Finally, we refer the Trial Chamber to the article of Mr. Roberts. Again this is included in our book of authorities. "What is military occupation. Here he refers to the Ansar Prison case from 1983. In the Ansar Prison case, the Supreme Court of Israel considered the -- whether an occupation existed in a refugee camp in Beirut when Israeli defence forces were present in Beirut during the hostilities there, when they were working with Christian Phalangist forces that carried out a massacre of Palestinians in a refugee camp. Again, it's another source of authority for the proposition that the classic belligerent occupation that counsel appears to require does not, in fact, have to be shown for there to be a state of occupation. Next slide. Defence argue that armed conflict and occupation are mutual exclusive. "They cannot co-exist." That's clearly incorrect. Even in the case of the classic belligerent occupation, obviously when Germany occupied Poland or France, there was still an armed conflict taking place. What counsel's, I believe, stating here is that there cannot be a state of occupation when you've got fighting in the territory where the occupation is supposedly taking place, and that's not correct. We refer the Trial Chamber to our final trial brief on that, paragraph 92, footnote 145. The existence of pockets of resistance does not negate an occupation if the other factors and requirements of occupation under the law are being met. Finally, the Defence asserts - this is point number 4 - that a military commander lacks executive power unless specifically tasked with it. And, Your Honours, the Prosecution respectfully disagrees with that assertion. We direct Your Honours to page 1272 of the Hostages case from Nuremberg, talking about the obligation, the duty, responsibility of the commanding general of occupied territory. "This not only applies to control of inhabitants in the accomplishment of these purposes, but the control and regulation of all other lawless persons or groups. He cannot escape responsibility by a claim of a want of authority. The authority is inherent in his position as commanding general of occupied territory. The primary responsibility for the prevention and punishment of crime lies with the commanding general; a responsibility from which he cannot escape by denying his authority over the perpetrators." There's further elaboration on this point, Your Honours, in the High Command case, page 544. "... but we are also of the opinion that under international law and accepted usages of civilised nations that he has certain responsibilities which he cannot set aside or ignore by reason of activities of his own state within the area -- his area. He is the instrument by which the occupancy exists. It is his army which holds the area in subjection. It is his might which keeps an occupied territory from re-occupancy by the armies of the nation to which it inherently belongs." Mr. President; Your Honours, the Prosecution would submit that this text is especially applicable in this case when considering the testimony of General Praljak and the assertion that he didn't have authority, the assertions repeated by Defence counsel in closing arguments, this assertion that the general's only responsible for the front line. And the general, in fact, is holding the territory, and it's by virtue of holding the territory that in this case many of the crimes committed against the civilians were able to take place. Finally, we refer the Trial Chamber to the extensive evidence in our view that shows that indeed Generals Petkovic and Praljak exercised extensive authority over these territories. Mr. President, Your Honours, in summary, the Prosecution asserts that both the facts and the law establish that Generals Petkovic and Praljak possessed and exercised authority as commanders of occupied territory. In his submissions on this, General Praljak's counsel, Mr. Kovacic, claimed that the Prosecution is asking too much of the Trial Chamber and that the Trial Chamber should resist the Prosecution's efforts to push the law in this direction. That's at page 52447 and 48 of the transcript from last week. We are not asking the Trial Chamber to push the law. We are asking you to faithfully apply it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We are not asking the Trial Chamber to push the law. We are asking you to faithfully apply it. What is the Defence asking the Trial Chamber when they ask you not to go down this road? A group of individuals carves out a new autonomous territory, a line on ethnic grounds. They take control of the territory, first politically and militarily. They replace the lawful civilian authorities. They defend the territory in armed conflict against the lawful armed forces of that territory. They pass scores of laws. They round up and detain hundreds of civilians in early May 1993, imprisoning them for a few weeks for their own safety. They intern the entire able-bodied male population. They detain, imprison, evacuate, transfer, and eventually deport much of the civilian population. They appropriate civilian property and housing stock. They control the roads. Is no one responsible to protect the civilians in this place? None of these gentlemen has stepped forward. If not them, then who? When the Defence ask you not to consider the issue of occupied territory, they don't want you to think about a very basic question, which was: Who was responsible for protecting the civilians? Now, Mr. President, Your Honours, it's the Prosecution submission that the HVO was in a position to exert its authority over these places that we say are occupied territory. They are expressly laid out, identified in the brief, specific places, specific periods of time. There was a state of occupation in these areas when Your Honours apply the facts and the law in this case. It was an international armed conflict. And for these reasons, Your Honours, we submit that despite the assertions made by the Defence, there was a state of occupation in an international armed conflict and this duty, then, does flow to the commanding generals who were in charge at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stringer. We have another 20 minutes before the break. Mr. Scott, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we switch to Sanction, please. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning each of Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel, all those in and around the courtroom who are assisting us. In responding to various points made during the Defence closings, there were three broad points or broad themes that ran through a number of the six closings. I'll identify specific examples as I go, but one of them was -- and many of these we relate -- the Prosecution submits relates what might be called more generally the Herceg-Bosna mythology, the mythology that has built up around Herceg-Bosna in an attempt to either justify it or to explain in an inaccurate and, we suggest, false way what was happening, what was going on with Herceg-Bosna. The Herceg-Bosna political mythology, if you will. The first -- the first dimension of that is that there is a repeated sense of right, a repeated presumption of correctness, of validity to -- that if the Croats put something forward, if one of the Herceg-Bosnans put a position forward, somehow that -- just by the fact that it's been put forward, it is presumptively correct. It is presumptively valid. It has the same equal weight or legitimacy as the decision or policy of a politically legitimate, legally recognised body. For example, Mr. Karnavas said on the 15th of February at transcript 52250: "And there is documentation, and maybe we'll get to that where they [referring to the Muslims] also have aspirations to get to the sea." Well, what it's underlying premise in that assertion? That the Muslims didn't have a right to get to the sea on their own sovereign international territory, but it's just a presumption that somehow the Bosnian Croats had a right to exclude the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina from its own territory. There was a second example during Ms. Alaburic's closing on the 21st of February, and I only have the daily transcript reference, my apology. When I was making my notes on that day it was on transcript page 25. There is an undisputed fact, she said, that in April 1993, the BH Army enlarged the territory under its control. If we totally ignore the question who started the conflict, we will agree that the BH Army was taking new territories, and that the area marked green here, the areas marked green, are getting larger, whereas the areas marked blue, controlled by the HVO, are getting smaller. Again, Ms. Alaburic just presumes, takes it as a given, that somehow that territory -- that's territory that belonged to Herceg-Bosna and the HVO, which it did not, not for one minute. Every bit of territory that she showed us on the maps, whether it was green or blue or pink, every bit of it belonged to the internationally recognised sovereign state of BiH. Not one square centimetre belonged to Herceg-Bosna. I also note here, and just to connect back to Mr. Stringer's arguments, the connection addressed to the notion of occupied territory, the whole notion that the ABiH was regaining territory, was gaining more territory, has within it the assertion, in fact the admission, that the HVO had occupied territory and it was only the BH that was regaining territory, regaining occupied territory, territory occupied by the HVO. It was Herceg-Bosna and the HVO and its sponsor and controlling state, Croatia, had occupied and controlled that territory, which was the very reason, the very circumstance which required the ABiH to "gain" new territory. It's own territory. But back to the main point. This whole attitude, this presumption of right, this automatic assumption of validity as if something is somehow a given, was noted by Judge Trechsel in an intervention with Mr. -- during Mr. Petkovic' testimony on the 11th of February, 2010. "Judge Trechsel: Mr. Petkovic, listening to you, one gets the impression that it was a matter of course that the authorities would be Croat, but that may be the issue, to establish Croat rule even where previously, as in Stolac, there was not a Croat rule and even a clear Muslim majority in the population." There was a similar or related posture which I will refer to as "Croat exceptionalism," that is the notion that, "The usual rules don't apply to us. It's okay for us to do something, but not for anyone else to do it." And we heard at that again during closing arguments. It's okay for the Croats to raise funds in foreign countries. It's okay for the Croats to bring volunteers which when they talk about the Muslims they use the term "foreign fighters." Well, foreign fighters are people who come from outside Bosnia, including all the Croats, all the volunteers, all the people from the Croatian diaspora, those were foreign fighters. But this attitude is it's okay for us to do that, but not for the Muslims to bring "foreign fighters." It was okay for the HVO to insist on a single military under a single command under the same supreme commander in Herceg-Bosna, but it was not okay for the legal BiH authorities to assert the same position. A third area of -- a continuing area of human -- concern throughout many of the Defence arguments was inconsistent or contradictory positions, depending on the argument or position being advanced at the moment. For example, consider the Defence position on the Sarajevo or BiH authorities. On the one hand, in some context we are told this was a passive dysfunctional group, a group that couldn't and didn't do much of anything, the gang, if you will, who couldn't shoot straight. Those were the BiH authorities. On the other hand, on other occasions and when it suits the Defence in making another argument, we were told that this was a highly organised top-down Muslim juggernaut centrally directed out of Sarajevo and threatening everything Croat. Well, which was it? Is it the gang that couldn't shoot straight or is it the highly co-ordinated top-down Muslim juggernaut? A similar -- another example was the Defence -- was the reference to Sarajevo being cut off. When it suited them for Sarajevo to be cut off, it was cut off, but note the numerous occasions when they weren't dealing specifically with that issue, when the evidence would creep in, the evidence would come in that, well, in fact, there were frequent regular communications and the ability to communicate and transportation into and out of Sarajevo when necessary. I'm reminded of the one specifically example where the issue of some financial software came up, financial software, and it was needed from Sarajevo, and it was readily available. Mr. Tomic testified to that, T33745-46. Well, we got it, we needed this software. Well, how did you get it? We got it from Sarajevo. Again, the position shifted and changed depending upon the Defence argument being made at the moment. Now I'll come back to some of those aspects in -- in a few moments in terms of some other specific arguments, but I want to turn now to something actually that came up in the end of the closing arguments by Mr. Sahota, and that was he reminded us -- and I certainly have no basis to disagree with him. He referred back to his training and work as an historian, and in doing so, he argued that, really, a case such as this really shouldn't be at the Tribunal, that these are really decisions for history to make and really not appropriate for adjudication, international courts shouldn't be about this business. Your Honour, the Prosecution strongly disagrees with that. In fact, it is truly a claim, a plea for impunity, that we should go back to the old days. These cases are too big. We can't hold leaders responsible. They are too complex. Let's just go back. We'll do camp guards and we'll do local commanders, but we can't possibly hold the top senior -- the top and senior political and military leaders responsible. It's just too difficult. The cases are too big. It's not appropriate for courts to do that, so let's give those people impunity. The Prosecution, with great respect, rejects that Defence argument. The Prosecution's pleading of a joint criminal enterprise in this case and the common objectives and the common purposes that were involved, it was fully 100 per cent consistent with the ICTY jurisprudence and practice. And in the interest of time, I'm not going to stop and read these, but as we go forward, I did go back over the weekend and re-read some of the trial judgements in other cases that dealt with the question of JCE. And I'll just remind you, and the Chamber will have these citations, the Krajisnik trial judgement, paragraph 1089. I'll just hit a few of these lightly. "The Bosnian-Serb leadership wanted to ethnically recompose the territories under its control by expelling and thereby drastically reducing the proportion of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats living there. 'Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities.'" The Chamber found those allegations to be proven. The Martic trial judgement, paragraph 442. I'll leave the Chamber to look at that language at paragraph 442. Sounds remarkably similar to the indictment in this case. "... the forcible removal of a majority of the Croat, Muslim and other non-Serb population from approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia and large parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to make them part of a new Serb-dominated state." Martic, paragraph 443. Martic, paragraph, trial judgement, 445. I'll pause on that one, at the end of paragraph 445, where the Chamber says and the Chamber's saying this has been proved, in the Trial Chamber's view this has been proved. "... the implementation of the political objective to establish a unified Serb territory in these circumstances necessitated the forcible removal of the non-Serb population from the SAO Krajina and the RSK territory. The Trial Chamber therefore finds beyond reasonable doubt that the common purpose of the JCE was the establishment of an ethnically Serb territory through the displacement of Croat and other non-Serb population ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt very quickly just to make the record, because I think that the reasonable, objective observer at this point in time cannot but conclude that the Trial Chamber is allowing the Prosecutor to make another closing argument and going into areas which are outside of the main of a rebuttal, and I do find this not just to be an abuse of process but also it dangerously comes close to an abuse of judicial discretion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm responding specifically to Mr. -- specific example to Mr. Sahota's argument. That this was not appropriate, that somehow this was too big a JCE, it was not appropriate under ICTY practice or should not be. I'm specifically responding to that argument. And I think the Defence, with great respect to my colleagues, is being overly narrow with its interpretation. The Prosecution, in good faith, stood up last week and gave -- and presented an outline of those things -- those topics that we wish to address. We listed them, got up and listed them. There was then argument about that. The Chamber decided to give us the three hours. On the basis of that ruling and on the basis of the representations that we made on Thursday, and I can go through the list again if necessary, once again the Prosecution, Mr. Stringer and I, worked long and hard since last Thursday to make this presentation. Now we're not doing that just because we have nothing else to do. We're trying to assist the Chamber. We believe that these are fair responses, these are fair responses, to the arguments raised. We don't know when the -- when we came into this three weeks ago, we didn't know what issues specifically the Defence would raise, what -- how they would use their time and their arguments. Yes, maybe some things were mentioned in their brief, would they use their five hours to address those, would they maybe put a new emphasis on something, would they take things in a slightly different direction, would we then for sure, Oh, this is really what they're focusing on, this is really now what they're focusing on, and therefore there is appropriate opportunity -- there should be an appropriate opportunity to respond, and the Chamber made that ruling last Thursday. We prepared accordingly, and everything I've said so far is in specific -- specific response to Defence arguments, including the citations I've given so far and including the argument made by Mr. Sahota. So I would like to be able to proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, but please each time refer to what the Defence argued during their closing arguments. Give us the transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will finish my response to Mr. Sahota's response and I'm just going to give you the citations. The Milutinovic -- well, I'm sorry. Ms. Winner reminds me I need to go back and make one correction. On the Krajisnik trial judgement, I apparently by error referred to paragraph 1089 and I should make it clear that the part I read was at page 1090, but I refer the Chamber to page -- paragraphs, excuse me, paragraphs 1089, 1090. My apology. I would also refer to the Chamber to the Milutinovic trial judgement, volume 3, paragraph 95; to the Djordjevic judgement, just last week, just last week, on the 23rd of February, 2011, I refer the Chamber to paragraphs 2000 and 2130. Again, the Trial Chamber making findings and describing the joint criminal enterprises in that case in language very similar to what would apply in this case. I'm now going to respond to an argument by Mr. -- perhaps we can do this before the break. I'm going now to respond to an argument made by Mr. Karnavas and specifically, Your Honour, it was made at transcript page 52254 and many other places, but that's one example that I'm going to give the Chamber when he addressed the evidence of Mr. Thornberry, but he was making a broader point, and it's a point to which the Prosecution wishes to respond and it fits into this notion about pleading and proving the joint criminal enterprise. Various of the Defence teams, but in particular Mr. Karnavas, have attacked the international witnesses in general, that is the witnesses from UNPROFOR, ECMM, the UNMOs, and other international organisations as having been either uninformed or misinformed and/or misguided, that they were all given or predisposed to a particular view or views, including the view that Herceg-Bosna was part of a Greater Croatia project directed from Zagreb. Now, let me give the specific example in response, Mr. President, to your request for transcript reference. 52254, Mr. Karnavas says: "Now, Mr. Thornberry ... he is at the top of the food chain at least for UNPROFOR and civil affairs, and of course his view was that everybody knew, it was a fact of life, it was a fact of life, that Croats were trying to ... carve out a piece of BiH. Well, if that's what people are getting planted into their mind at the very top when they first arrived for their orientation and then they arrive at the scene, that's the prism by which they will all view the events. Very few were capable of seeing past that." And that's just one example, but that wasn't limited -- this position was not limited to Mr. Thornberry. The Prosecution submits that the Defence arguments in this respect are all based on a fundamentally false premise, and that is that internationals were misinformed. The Prosecution would submit, Your Honours, that in fact the evidence in this case compellingly supports the view, the notion, the conclusion, that the internationals were exactly right. The internationals and their assessments over the years, through from 1992 to 1995, made assessments about what was happening, and what Herceg-Bosna was about, and about Greater Croatia, and about Tudjman's agenda. It's not that they were misguided. The evidence in this case shows that they were right. I'm not going to take the Chamber's time to go through all the evidence, but I'm just going to quickly pass through it. I'll give the Chamber the references if the Chamber wants to go back through them. Tudjman's own words which the Chamber has heard repeatedly. Prlic's own words that we've heard repeatedly. There was a plan directed from Zagreb. Praljak's testimony, "We wanted borders. We wanted a Croat area with borders that would be permanent." Boban's words, "We are at war over territory and borders." Akmadzic: We want "Herceg-Bosna, with borders," et cetera. The fundamental notion that the internationals were "misinformed" is just simply wrong. The evidence in this case shows that the internationals were correctly informed. Your Honours, on that point it looks like the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. We need to have a break. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. The Trial Chamber is telling the Prosecution that it has one hour and 30 minutes left -- 38 minutes left for the rebuttal, and after that the Trial Chamber will ask each Defence how long they need for their rejoinder, possibly, of course, because it could also waive its right to a rejoinder. We also would like to remind you that Mr. Karnavas will have 15 minutes because he was told that he could he give us his point of view after last week's hearings. And then also we would like the Defence to tell us whether the accused wish to take the floor. As you know, the accused are entitled to take the floor at the very end. So they will have -- the counsel for Defence will have to tell us whether their clients want to take the floor or not. We also ask Mr. Scott to be very careful and to always cite his sources, especially the transcript pages where such and such Defence would have proffered such and such words. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I want to turn ever so briefly to the question of the Prosecution witnesses. All six of the Defence teams spent considerable parts of their closing arguments attacking in various respects virtually all the Prosecution witnesses and their credibility. If I was going to respond to all of that, it would literally take, well, all of three hours and then some, but let me just pick a couple as examples, simply to say -- just to remind the Chamber and ask the Chamber just as the -- just as the Defence did, not to accept counsel's assertions, either mine or theirs, simply at face value, but of course to look back at the evidence. Now, let me give the Chamber two examples. Mr. Karnavas spent time attacking the evidence of the constitutional expert Dr. Ribicic, and that was at transcript 52241 and following. I think Mr. Karnavas's, with all due respect, treatment of Dr. Ribicic was unfair. Can I remind the Chamber that Dr. Ribicic was a Rule 92 bis witness. We presented his transcript and from the Kordic case, and given that, he was not asked to do any new or additional work. That is the nature of a Rule 92 bis witness. We presented him to the Court to be considered with the similar evidence of the viva voce expert, Mr. Tomljanovich. Contrary to what counsel have said, Dr. Ribicic did submit an entirely bona fide expert report in which, in fact, he did exactly what Mr. Karnavas repeatedly said that the Prosecution should have done, and that is, Dr. Ribicic, as a constitutional scholar, as a sitting judge, by the way, on the Slovenian Constitutional Court, went through the Herceg-Bosna legislation, the Herceg-Bosna papers, the very work that Mr. Karnavas said should be done, carefully examined that documentation, and I might mention that documentation didn't change. There wasn't new Herceg-Bosna law between his Kordic testimony and his Prlic testimony. He examined all the existing HVO documentation, Herceg-Bosna documentation, and provided his conclusions in his report. I just simply say -- ask Your Honours to take Dr. Ribicic's evidence, if you will, as a 92 bis witness who then came for cross, and Mr. Tomljanovich's viva voce evidence, take their evidence together with the other evidence in the case and we submit that it is fully credible and fully persuasive. The only other example I'll pause on is the international witness Mr. Pellnas, Bo Pellnas, the Swedish military observer or UNPROFOR officer. For some reason a number of the accused attacked Mr. Pellnas's evidence. I'll just remind the Chamber of what Mr. Filipovic, a Defence witness who had actual encounters with Mr. Pellnas during the time, said. Mr. Filipovic at transcript 47770-71. Mr. Filipovic, in an unsolicited assessment, when context -- when a context came up involving Mr. Pellnas said, and I'm quoting Mr. Filipovic, Pellnas was "a true professional." A true professional. Now let's turn again, ever so briefly, to the credibility of the Defence witnesses. The Prosecution again has had to use its limited pages and limited time as wisely as we thought possible, as wisely as our judgements could make and maybe we were wrong. Maybe we make good judgements. Maybe we made bad judgements, but we had to allocate our time as best we thought. Therefore, we did not spend a great deal of time or pages addressing the credibility of the Defence witnesses, some but not many. The Chamber, of course, will have to make its own assessments of the credibility of each witness and what weight, if any, and I stress if any, to give to his or her evidence. With respect, with great respect, the Prosecution submits that there was hardly a Defence witness who was not substantially impeached, weakened, and/or contradicted on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do apologise for interrupting and I've tried to sit quietly throughout the speech of the Prosecution. Your Honours have enjoined on a number of occasions that the Prosecution be specific, and it seems that despite that enjoinder, my learned friend is seeking repeatedly to make general statements to paint with a broad brush. Another way of putting it perhaps is to use a butcher's knife to the issue of rebuttal when a surgeon's scalpel was needed, and I would ask that a forensic approach be adopted. When it comes to the Defence witnesses for Stojic, everything we've said is supported in our final brief, and we're going to take a very strict line if the Prosecution, at any stage, wish to address anything in relation to Mr. Stojic because everything we've -- apart from one or two matters on sentencing, everything else, in fact, has been covered in our final brief. Your Honours, my learned friend Mr. Stringer earlier prayed in aid the Naletilic and Martinovic case in relation to occupation and yet, of course, the Prosecution, I'm sure, would not seek to turn away from that case when it comes to the clear case law of Judge Liu, which I referred to on the weekend. And it's very clear that rebuttal is not an opportunity to reinforce the Prosecution's case, and yet that's what -- that's precisely what it seems the Prosecution is trying to do. So, Your Honour, I would ask that rather than -- I won't call them platitudes, but rather than general assertions, the Prosecution be specific and address particular averments made by the Defence when it comes to Defence witnesses because, as I said earlier, our submissions in relation to the credit of Defence witnesses and their testimony has all been briefed in our final brief. And there's nothing, we say, that the Prosecution can say about Mr. Stojic that would legitimately and properly come within the scope of rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admittedly, Mr. Scott, the Defence teams have quoted their own witnesses. There was Skender and Andabak and others, there are other Defence witnesses. Since you're now dealing with this issue, tell us as much as possible the details. Witness so-and-so said at page so-and-so, and for us, as Prosecution, their evidence has no probative value, but we need to have the exact references because, of course, we took notes as we went along. We're going to look into the transcript and the record, but we need to have the exact reference pages where you criticise this or that Defence witness, because you rightly said it will be for the Trial Chamber to assess the probative value of each and every Defence witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was about to turn to a couple of examples, but -- but let me just be very brief. I can't respond to every one. I simply want to ask the Chamber and remind the Chamber that, of course, the credibility of all witnesses, Prosecution and Defence, will have to be carefully assessed according to the evidence they gave. And the Chamber will recall in a number of instances, for example, the Defence -- there were a couple of Defence witness who came. One who denied Ustasha war crimes in World War II, that Jasenovac didn't really happen or should be greatly minimised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas -- Mr. Scott. Do you believe that you have to recall to the Chamber that it must critically assess the creditability of all witnesses? I would think this is such a basic, matter-of-fact character that rebuttal should not address such a broad general issue and sort of lecture the Chamber on how to do its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it certainly, Your Honour, was not meant as a lecture. I would agree with you whole-heartedly, in any event, Judge Trechsel, and it wouldn't matter whether I did, of course, or not, but I don't intend -- and if the Prosecution was to stand here for some time and go on with such a lecture, I would certainly agree that that would be inappropriate. Because of the interventions and this was -- really would have been a one-minute thing, just simply to remind that just as the Defence has implored and spent considerable time talking about the credibility of Prosecution witnesses, simply was intended to be a very brief passing reference to the fact that, of course, the same principles as the Chamber, as Judge Trechsel just mentioned, applied to the Defence as well. I will respond specifically because there was the specific response allegation or assertion that the Prosecution had attacked all Croat witnesses as somehow inappropriate or not believable. The Prosecution never, ever said that, would never say that. That simply is not the case. In fact, the Prosecution has referred to the evidence of or related to a number of moderate or more moderate Croats including Kljuic, Brkic, Pelivan, Markesic, Komsic, the Catholic archbishop in Sarajevo Mr. Vinko Puljic, et cetera. The Prosecution has never taken the position, as asserted by the Defence, oh, the Prosecution stood up and told you not to believe any Croat witnesses. That is not our position, has never been our position. Now as to the Herceg-Bosna insiders, and let me adopt Mr. Sahota's words, let me adopt Mr. Sahota's words, when he said, well, you know, some witnesses come with "an axe to grind." Well, I submit to the Chamber is ever so true, or may be ever so true, and for the Chamber's assessment as to the numerous witnesses who came that held high and senior positions in Herceg-Bosna and the HVO and whether they indeed in coming before this Chamber had an axe to grind. Your Honour, I do need to make one correction. In reference to some of the arguments made by Ms. Alaburic, there was an error, and when we find an error, we've certainly throughout the trial fessed up to it, if you will. In this regard, we confirm that in connection with an argument made by Ms. Alaburic that was in the Petkovic part of our final brief, there was an error in citation. In paragraph 937 of the Prosecution's final brief, we cited in footnote 2086, Exhibit P05308. The correct exhibit and citation is P02950, which is also cited on the same topic in other parts of the brief. They are two similar documents in many ways on the same topic and because they were cited a number of times, the two citations were switched. But if the Chamber will please note, and I'll say again, in footnote 286, the citation should be P02950, not P05308. Although both are ultimately relevant to the case. With that correction, the Prosecution argument is correct and fully supported that Mr. Petkovic was fully on notice based on the ICRC report prior to his forced labour order in July 1993. Your Honours, I'd now like to turn in response to arguments made by Mr. Karnavas at pages 52266 to 68 about the legitimacy of the BiH Presidency and Mr. Izetbegovic. He went on for some pages about that. Throughout the whole period starting in 19 -- in the earliest times and going up to 1990 -- to the third election, if you will, of Mr. Izetbegovic. From 1990 elections to the third term. Your Honour, I would submit to the Chamber -- and I'll try to take this somewhat more briefly than I had anticipated. As the Chamber reviews the evidence, there is abundant evidence, including from the Defence's own witnesses, that the -- the -- excuse me, the BiH Presidency and Mr. Izetbegovic's role in that Presidency as president was entirely legal, entirely valid, entirely legitimate from at least the period of the December 1990 election or formation of that first government to at least the end of 1993. And I submit to the Chamber and I'm going to be very bold about this because if the Chamber reviews the evidence, you'll find it, I'm confident, quite clear that despite all the words to the contrary, despite all the argument, the evidence in this case, from the witnesses and from the documents, is that the Presidency was completely valid throughout this time period. And Mr. Akmadzic himself, a high-level insider, a man who held a -- initially a nonpolitical position in the Presidency, then became prime minister, followed these events closely, was one of the senior Herceg-Bosna witnesses brought by the Defence. Mr. Akmadzic repeatedly said, as I took him through it from 1990 to the end of 1992 and 1993: "Mr. Akmadzic, let me make sure I understand you. You're saying that during that period the Presidency was legitimate? "Yes, that's right. "And how about 1992? "Yes, that's right." Now, if we go through some of the slides very quickly and I'm just -- because the Chamber will have the citations of Mr. Akmadzic's testimony, and I will mention -- I'm not going to mention any testimony at this moment but the other critical -- the other important witness on that point is Witness 1DAA. I'm not mentioning evidence at this point in connection, but I'm saying that if the Chamber reviews the Akmadzic evidence on this point and the Witness 1DAA evidence on this point, the evidence is completely clear. There was no question that Mr. -- for example, that President Izetbegovic's -- Izetbegovic was elected to a completely legal and valid term from December of 1990 to December of 1991. I'm going to come back to that in a moment and I probably should have done this differently, but so that I don't get lost, I'm going to step off that before I get lost and address something more or less chronologically, because we're now into 1991. Izetbegovic has been elected president and we've heard again during closing arguments and specifically, I think a number of times, but specifically by Mr. Khan on page 52309, Izetbegovic says this is not our war. Now, if -- I'll just simply try to remind the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do object. I do object. That's very clearly -- it couldn't be any clearer, that point is addressed in our final brief, and the Prosecution were enjoined in the Scheduling Order to respond to issues in our final brief. They had that opportunity, and this is not the occasion to reinforce arguments that they may be dissatisfied with simply because perhaps the Defence have highlighted some areas of difficulty that the Prosecution now are trying to repair. Your Honours, I would ask that Mr. Scott cease this attempt to open up a new closing speech via the back door of rebuttal. It is most inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't accept -- with all due respect, we don't accept that we're making a new closing speech. We're specifically responding -- I might as well say if it was in the closing -- if it was in the Defence closing brief and if the Prosecution didn't raise it in our oral submissions, which went first, then why did the Defence spend time on it in their closing submissions? I mean, that's the same -- that's the same logic. I think it's the same logic. And when they do respond, then when it is made and it is a point given emphasis to, whether we could not get to it perhaps in our 400 pages against 1.200 pages, that they choose to make an issue of it in their closing oral submissions that we have an opportunity to respond to that. I fail to see the unfairness of the Prosecution being allowed to respond to the arguments made in this way. I simply don't see -- I just simply don't what's unfair about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the greatest of respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we remind you that you have to state specifically what was said by a Defence team in their closing arguments on a specific topic and then you can say you don't agree with it and you can explain why you deem it's not fair, but you have to rely on their closing arguments in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I may add a point. I think Mr. Khan has absolutely correctly interpreted that -- the Chamber's ruling. Rebuttal is to answer issues raised orally, not to answer issues that are in the brief, because the opportunity to answer the issues in the brief, limited, of course, that is admitted, but that was in your final pleadings. So please concentrate on points that were arisen -- were raised orally but not already in the written final briefs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to do that as I go and I'll try to sort further on that basis. As I said before, the Prosecution prepared its -- its presentation today based on the ruling that we received last Thursday and thought that this was considered -- would be considered fair response, but I will try to make -- I will try to edit my comments as I go. I would simply on that point then, Your Honours, remind the Chamber of the evidence to that -- about that statement that the Chamber will be aware of, in particular the statement by Mr. Anton Tus, P10462, a senior Croat who clearly indicated and -- this statement was completely mischaracterised. Now, returning to the second term. I said that I was going to take -- taking a step off the Presidency. Now, returning to that, as I said, there's no dispute that Mr. Izetbegovic was properly then elected to a second term in a fully legal and legitimate way. And Mr. Akmadzic confirmed that at T 29473-74. Now, as then events developed in April of 1992, with the declaration of the imminent state of war, at that time the Presidency consisted of the president, so Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Kljuic, Mr. Boras, and Mr. Ganic.
