Of course, around that time, the Serb members, Mr. Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic, had left given the outbreak of war with the Serbs, if you will, and there was the business of replacing those Serbs. But also on the Presidency at that time, because the expanded Presidency provided for the inclusion of not just the regular members but also the - excuse me, Your Honours - the president of the Assembly, the prime minister, and the military head of the BiH armed forces. At the time, that included Mr. Pelivan, the Croat prime minister; the minister of defence Mr. Doko, Jerko Doko, a Croat; and then the -- excuse me, and then the addition of the head of the ABiH armed forces. Now, there is no dispute about that. Excuse me, Your Honour. In the effort to cut through, I'm editing as I go. It was that Presidency as so -- as so comprised that again Mr. Akmadzic said, well, how about then? Was it legal and legitimate then? Well, yes, it was. And he cites that, and he talks about that among a number of places both at T29638-39 and T29641. Now if we could go into private session for a moment about a protected witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Registrar. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution will again just simply ask the Chamber to review again the evidence of Mr. Akmadzic, the -- the witness -- excuse me, the evidence of Mr. Okun. Also P00829. And the long and short of that evidence is that, in fact, what happened was there was agreement reached by late 1992 by Tudjman and Boban, saying, all right, fine, let Izetbegovic serve another term. And there are contemporaneous notes of that agreement or references to that agreement in Mr. Okun's notes, and Dr. -- Mr. Okun specifically said was, well, Tudjman referred to it as he would recommend to Boban that we let Izetbegovic have another term, but Okun says, We all knew what that really meant. When he word -- when he used the word "I recommend to Boban," we all knew what that really meant in so many words was "I've instructed Boban." And that's at page 16717 of Okun's testimony. At the end of the day, the point made by these events is that the -- in fact the BiH Presidency and Mr. Izetbegovic's role as president was completely valid and legitimate from December of 1990 at least to the end of 1993. The -- the most pertinent part of the times for references -- for purposes of this case. Excuse me, Your Honour. Now, I next want to turn to the point that was made by the Defence that during the spring of 1992, the Defence would have you believe that the HVO military was -- was the only organised military force that was fighting the Serbs and that Herceg-Bosna and the HVO was forced to organise itself because, you know, again, supposedly, the BiH authorities weren't doing anything. This was specifically asserted by Mr. Kovacic on the 17th of February, and again I only have the daily transcript reference, page 83. Mr. Khan, on the 15th of February, page 52309, which he said, for example, why does Bosnia-Herzegovina exist today? Who was the cavalry who was riding to the rescue of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera, et cetera. Ms. Nozica then touched on the issue on the 16th of February at daily transcript pages 27 and 28. Came up repeatedly. The response to those arguments, Your Honour, is that they're built again on a fundamentally false premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I again rise. That very issue has been again dealt with in our final brief in numerous places and I will just give one example. If one looks at 2.3.2, we said, very clearly, that -- we mention this very assistance and its importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the Trial Chamber insists once again, please make reference to what was said orally, not in written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just did that. I just gave the Chamber the references to the -- to the closing argument and pages. I can only -- I can only state them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this actually brings into quite stark relief the very fallacy, I think, with the greatest of respect, that is besetting the Prosecution. On numerous occasions the first point is the Prosecution's prayed in aid and, in fact, in my respectful submission, they're exposed because in response to the two interventions I've made so far, the Prosecution on both occasions has said, Well, Your Honours, we didn't have enough pages. Well, that's a complete red herring. That's absolutely impermissible. It's an irrelevant consideration, as Mr. Kovacic said last week. Those matters are res judicata, and we cannot pray in aid matters that have been judicially decided. But, Your Honours, the various case law that was referred to on Thursday, the Halilovic case, Naletilic case, the jurisprudence is very clear. Judge Trechsel today and Your Honours by way of the legal officers prior to today made it very clear that the Prosecution should be disciplined and simply limit themselves to matters that have not been raised in substance in the Defence final briefs. And I made the submission and in my -- I maintain, with the greatest of respect, as a matter of law it's correct, unless a matter arises ex improviso that the Prosecution could not have reasonably expected, they have no right to make further rebuttal arguments or to make further submissions under the guise of rebuttal, and that's what's going on here. There are further submissions couched in general terms under the guise of rebuttal, and, Your Honours, we did raise this very assistance given by Croatia in our final brief many times. It's peppered throughout our brief. It's one of our constant themes. Whatever the Prosecution say, they can't say that the Stojic team has been inconsistent in this regard. And, Your Honours, I would ask that the Prosecution be brought into line and simply be told to properly focus rebuttal. Just because Your Honours have been most generous and given them three hours is not a licence for them to use those three hours in an impermissible manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please try to use the time you have left in a wise manner. The Trial Chamber believes that all lawyers, be it Defence lawyers or Prosecution, are all trying to assist the Trial Chamber. So please try and be very effective and help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to do that. I do and I must spend valuable time, at least a moment, to resist -- you know, for the last two weeks the Prosecution's been called dishonest, sleazy, unethical, et cetera, et cetera, for two weeks now. Well, repeatedly, repeatedly, and great licence was taken with mischaracterised evidence, not just the evidence that maybe was wrong or maybe there was a disagreement, but repeatedly, the things we've done wrong. And even now, on the one hand, Mr. Khan says, I'm not -- I don't want to attack counsel but essentially accuses me, in so many words, of bad faith. Now that's just not -- we don't accept that. We're trying to assist the Chamber. We're not trying to abuse the process. We're not trying to take licence. We're trying to assist the Chamber. And there is some -- while we believe -- let me be very clear, let me be very clear. We believe that we're well within the scope of a permissible rebuttal and the discretion of this Chamber to allow what is helpful to the Chamber and I think that the rules that have been cited are too narrow, are being characterised as far too narrow. So we believe we're within it. But I do have to say and I do have to make a record, I'm sorry because I didn't want to get to this point, but when counsel said, Well, you know, it's too bad they couldn't respond to that. When we had a third of as many pages in time, they got 1200 pages to raise every issue in the book and we got 400 pages, when they get 30 hours and we get 15 hours, I think it's only fair. The Prosecution get a limited amount of time, my goodness, three hours, not days, three hours to respond to very specific points that have been raised. I think that's entirely fair and entirely appropriate, and I don't accept the Prosecution is acting in bad faith or trying to take licence where there is none. It's inappropriate. The Prosecution is trying to assist the Chamber. If the Chamber don't find it helpful, the Prosecution can certainly sit down and we'll be done and our work will be done. If the Chamber don't find it helpful, I'm sorry for that. This is to assist the Chamber. Our concern is -- quite frankly, our concern is that there's a number of issues the Prosecution hadn't been able to fully address, and we want to assist the Chamber in putting that evidence together and putting those arguments together so that we're trying to assist the Chamber. But if the Chamber don't want the assistance, it makes it -- obviously it's the Chamber -- I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, that's nice to hear. I just think that if everyone were given permission to assist the Chamber until they have exhausted their ways of assisting, I think we would sit here for another year and here in closing arguments one after the other. So I must say in this point I agree with Mr. Khan. The ruling of this phase in the game is that you answer points which were not raised in the written submissions but only came up as an oral argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I'll be governed accordingly. I would only say no one is suggesting, no one is claiming that this process should go on forever. The Chamber has given us the three hours. When the three hours is up, it's over. It doesn't go on for days or years, it goes on for the next hour and some minutes. So it's not, with all due respect, completely fair to say that we're just endlessly extending the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I take that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We've tried to be selective and within that limited three hours to think what would be of most assistance to the Chamber, but I take it on board. I'm directed accordingly. In that regard, Your Honours, let me review -- well, if the Chamber would just allow me, then, to complete on that topic just the most summary statement. Review the evidence of Mr. Petkovic and review the evidence of Mr. Filipovic because both of them came in here, sat there and told you under oath there was no HVO military in April. They got there. They arrived in mid-April. There was no army. There was no military. They organised it and they told you exactly where the ABiH stood at the same time as well. And there was -- the HVO had no advantage. In fact, they said within a very short time, in fact, the ABiH was bigger, had more professional officers, et cetera. So review the evidence. Review the Petkovic and Filipovic evidence before you assume that, well, there wasn't -- the HVO was somehow miles ahead and that's how and that's why they had no choice but to go with the HVO. Not the case at all. Your Honour, during the closing arguments Mr. Kovacic said, on the 17th of February, at daily transcript page 86, again raising the argument that the HVO was somehow -- HVO military was somehow a legitimate part of the BiH armed forces. Obviously this is a point on which the parties continue to strongly disagree. If the Chamber would allow me one brief response in lieu of some pages of evidence to the contrary. The key issue here is what Izetbegovic said at the 21 July 1992 meeting and that's P00336, page 60. Izetbegovic couldn't have made it clearer that, on the one hand, while rejecting Herceg-Bosna completely, absolutely completely, we do not accept, we will not accept Herceg-Bosna, he then says the HVO military is "not only acceptable but it is also necessary and of course desirable in all ways." That is, if you join us, we're happy to have you, but you truly have to become part of the same armed force. The Prosecution -- let me be very clear, the Prosecution does not run from that language. The Prosecution embraces that language. What the evidence shows, what all the Presidential transcripts and all the meeting records show throughout this period is that Izetbegovic and the BiH Presidency was continuously reaching out, trying to bring the HVO in. Yes, we want you, please do come in, but you've got to be part of the same army, you can't have it both ways. We want to be part of you, but we want to have another supreme commander over here named Boban. We want to have another oath. We want to have -- serve a different agenda, but on the other hand, we're part of you. That is the issue. And again, I direct the Chamber's attention in particular -- I invite the Chamber's attention to P00336. The MTS issue and again it was raised by almost everyone, Mr. Khan on the 15th of February, Mr. Karnavas, Ms. Nozica, Mr. Kovacic, Mr. Praljak himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, once again, I have been very careful, we have been very careful, and mindful of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that's more than nine, ten years old. This case law goes back to 2002. It's not new, and it predates even the further clarification provided by the Bench today and yesterday, and the other point, Your Honour, of course, is that the subjective views of the parties as to fairness, we think this being fair or the Prosecution being that, so-and-so being fair is irrelevant. Fortunately, we are not the arbiters of fairness. Your Honours are. But the issue of MTS has been dealt with extensively in our final trial brief. For example, paragraphs 37, 38, and it goes on and on and on. Your Honour, it's been dealt with extensively. If you look generally at 2.3.2 again, the whole section deals with MTS. The Prosecution simply do not have a proper basis to address Your Honours on this, and, Your Honours, it's very easy for my learned friend to prove me wrong. It's very easy. It just requires a little bit of pause. Let the Prosecution point to the new issue that we raise in our oral submissions that was not included in our brief. If they do that and say, well, Mr. Khan said this, the Stojic team said this in their oral submissions and that is not founded upon our final brief, of course they would have a proper basis arguably for addressing the Bench, leaving aside the matter whether or not it was reasonably foreseeable. But, Your Honours, the Prosecution's not doing that. Despite the injunctions given, they're once again ploughing on, impervious, it seems, to the injunctions of the Trial Chamber under the rubric of editing, but they are continually addressing matters that we heard when Mr. Scott opened. And, Your Honours, in my respectful submission, it's not a case of them having three hours, as I mentioned before. It's whether or not Mr. Scott's submissions are proper -- properly fall under the scope of rebuttal or if he is inadvertently or deliberately seeking to expand the proper scope of rebuttal. Your Honour, if it's the latter, I'd ask that the -- well, either way I would ask that the Bench ask -- require the Prosecution to put forward focused and limited submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just one sentence. The issue of MTS that my dear colleague is now starting to talk was raised even pre-trial briefs. It was litigated during the trial and it was mentioned in final brief, as my dear colleague said. Nobody has raised anything new and added anything to this -- to those facts during the oral presentation, nobody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it seems that we have spent hundreds of hours on MTS. Though as Mr. Khan says, what we're interested in is anything new during the closing arguments on MTSs, which would require a response or a rebuttal from you, but it has to be new, something new during the closing arguments, not something that was written in their closing arguments, in the trial briefs. In the final briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will then -- I will not address it further except to say that again we were -- and I can't give the Chamber a specific citation for this, but I remember well sitting here these last two weeks and being accused of the Prosecution having simply ignored that evidence, and as if we -- that it amounts to come concession, some admission that we just recklessly ignored this evidence. It seems to me that the Prosecution should have a chance to respond to those positions, but apparently not. I would remind the Chamber as to the two meetings -- two of the meetings with Mr. Mladic in which the positions taken by the accused in that meeting were quite contrary to simply -- freely providing MTS. Various statements saying denying them food, bringing the Muslims to their knees, we are not giving them ammunition, we're not giving them anything, dramatically contrary to positions taken in this courtroom. But the Chamber has that evidence. Let me try this one see if it's -- this is fair or not because right now I'm not -- it's not always entirely clear. But perhaps this is -- I can respond to this comment by Defence counsel during closing. Ms. Nozica at one point in -- in the part of her argument denying that Mr. Stojic had any military power made reference to Mr. Prlic cosigning a mobilisation order and the argument -- this is at page 52319 to 22. Now, this was specifically raised and argued in closing and said, well, that's just evidence that Mr. Stojic didn't have any military powers, the fact that Mr. Prlic had to sign it in order to give it some authority. Well, Your Honour, obviously that says a lot about what Mr. Stojic, if that's correct, thought about Mr. Prlic's power. And I think it's fair to say and I think that raises a broader point that I don't think has been addressed specifically before and I invite the Chamber's attention to it --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is a misinterpretation. The Stojic Defence never alleged that Mr. Prlic was required to sign a mobilisation order. That's a misinterpretation. I have the page in front of me. If my learned friend is prepared, then they can find the relevant page themselves. The Stojic Defence submits that the order to implement mobilisation must have been cosigned by Mr. Prlic, not by -- that Mr. Stojic didn't have the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I hope you took due note of what Ms. Nozica just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do note, Your Honour, and the Chamber of course will decide what the evidence says of those pages that I gave to the Chamber a few minutes ago. The important point is and I do ask the Chamber to consider this as it considers the evidence, and I don't think it's a point that's been made before, how did each of those accused view and deal with each other during the relevant time? How did each of these accused deal with each other during this time period? Because that can tell the Chamber a great deal about the powers and the positions and the responsibility they held. If Mr. -- if -- assuming that my interpretation or understanding of the evidence is correct, if Mr. Stojic thought it was only Mr. Prlic who could give authority to this order, doesn't that tell us something about what Mr. Stojic thought about Mr. Prlic's power and responsibility at the time? The Chamber should consider that and I submit these men, all six of them, treated each other as important and powerful participants at the upper levels of the Herceg-Bosna political and military leadership. They treated each other accordingly, just as Mr. Stojic recognised Mr. Prlic's authority in having him co-signe the mobilisation order. That's how they viewed each other at the time. It wasn't, oh, I don't have any power, I don't know, I have no position, I have no influence. They all treated each other as people as senior people with great powers and great positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, when you're going through it, I'm not going to belabour the point. I've made my observations. I know my learned friend for the Prosecution says that there's difficulties knowing the rules. The rules are very clear. The Prosecution should rely and cite that aspect of the oral arguments that have not been raised in our final brief. Now, Your Honours, if you look at page 52320, we do address Article 7 of the decree of armed forces and the issue of mobilisation, and, Your Honour, that issue in general is dealt with in 3.2.2.2 of our final brief. And, Your Honour, we referred to P03038, and, Your Honours, that document is referred to in the Prosecution's final brief at paragraph 540, and, Your Honour, of course there is a reference of the 8th of February transcript, page 41. So, Your Honours, once again there's nothing new in relation to the submission that was made that is not founded upon our final brief. Your Honours -- it's for Your Honours to decide whether or not Mr. Scott can continue repeatedly in this vein, but as far as the assertion that the rules are unclear. They could not be any clearer. The Prosecution should be required to say at transcript page 52320, the Prosecution -- the Defence said this and that has not been raised in their final brief. If they can't make that second link that it was not raised in their final brief, they do not have the right, under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, to address the Bench again. Your Honours, we cannot accept some jurisprudence we like and ignore the parts that somehow limit us. Your Honours, that's not the proper way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the rebuttal is not an opportunity to have another go, another bite of the cherry. You are supposed to counter closing arguments. You have to challenge what was said in court, within that stage of the proceedings. And I believe this is the unanimous view of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In case there's some further intervention. Excuse me. My apologies for not having the microphone on. I was just observing the Chamber whether there was -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had intended, and perhaps the Chamber can tell me if they think it's a fair topic or not, I also had intended to address the arrest of the Muslim men on the 30th of June and the particular view expressed by Ms. Alaburic that would have the Chamber believe that, you know, the world essentially sprang into existence on the 30th of June, as if all the things leading up to that event had not happened. But if the Chamber doesn't think that's appropriate for further comment, then I won't address it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I with like to say a sentence. As we are talking about the 30th of June, 1993, the Petkovic Defence dedicated to that date a lot of time in their final brief and the same goes for the Prosecution. We also spoke about it at length in our closing argument. We have not heard a single new argument, and we did not say anything new with regard to what was written in our final brief. We have said everything about the date, and there's no need to tackle the issue in the rebuttal. In general terms, if my learned friend Mr. Scott thinks that there is a new thesis, I would kindly invite him to present that new thesis rather than broach the subject of the 30th of June in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. We're going to discuss the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, regarding the 30th of June, what was new about it in the closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I wanted to respond specifically, Your Honours, to the closing argument emphasis on the role of the -- of the alleged Muslim members of the HVO and their arrest and the position taken about that and remind the Chamber of the evidence by Mr. Filipovic on that point, which I believe is contrary to the Defence position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me repeat that this has been belaboured at length in our final brief, and we believe that this has been done and dusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The presence of Muslims within the HVO is a topic that has been addressed numberless times. Also in the filings and briefs. What was there in court that was said that was new coming from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, it's -- it's part of the difficulty is to say, of course, topics, of course broad topics have been raised. There is -- there's virtually nothing, presumably, that's been said that's entirely a new topic after five years, but it's responding to specific aspects of those topics, specific issues that have been emphasised and put and emphasised during closing argument and that is what the Prosecution has tried to respond to. Certainly the topic of the 30th of June has been raised before. No doubt about that. But there are specific aspects of it that we had hoped to be able to address further, but we won't. As to the status, though, if I can just come back to some of the statements that -- arguments that Mr. Stringer made and I would just invite the Chamber to look at the evidence of Mr. Filipovic as to the status and the right of Muslim members of the HVO to leave, just as he left the -- he and others left the JNA when they determined that the JNA was the enemy. I asked Mr. Filipovic didn't Muslims have exactly the same right to leave the HVO, and Mr. Filipovic said yes, they did, and that's repeatedly throughout his testimony. If I can respond, Your Honour, to one specific Petkovic exhibit and then I'll wrap up my remarks if I'm allowed. Ms. Alaburic spent considerable time on Exhibit P00279, which she says is -- or asserts is a speech, a text of an oral speech --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, I really need to intervene at this point. This document refers to a speech which was not delivered. In their final brief, the Prosecutor has attempted to show that General Petkovic was involved in certain discussions on political issues, and one and the same document reappears and is being belaboured, and the speech was never delivered. Your Honours, this is nothing new. This is not a new topic. In my final brief, I have elaborated the topic at great length, and I have explained everything that is of some relevance for that topic. In my closing argument, I didn't say anything new with this regard. Some of it was in response to the closing argument by the Prosecution. So this is indeed a very old topic which has been belaboured at great length by the Prosecution as well as by me. In other words, there is nothing new about the topic, and if I am mistaken, maybe Mr. Scott can tell us if there is anything new, but I believe that it is wrong for him to reiterate the Prosecutor's position on a speech which was never delivered. It is true that the speech was not delivered. It was proven, and if my learned friends have ever considered it challengeable, they should have disputed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a draft speech, wasn't it, Mr. Scott? And apparently, if we're to believe the Defence, it was never held as a speech. If you believe that this was a speech that was delivered as such, as part of your rebuttal you must tell us that you challenge the Defence's approach for specific reasons. Now, if you believe that the speech was never delivered, you should not insist on it as part of your rebuttal, because if there was no speech, those words are deemed never to have been uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this very exchange highlights the importance of being able to address these matters, because the Prosecution couldn't disagree more. And Ms. -- Ms. -- again this is an example where my good friend Ms. Alaburic gets up and makes an assertion that the Prosecution does not accept at all. She says it's true because she says so, that the speech was never delivered. Now the state of the evidence is the only person who supports clearly is Mr. Petkovic himself, and I won't belabour what the Prosecution's view of his credibility is. But the only other person who addressed that was Mr. Beneta, and Mr. Beneta specifically, at the end of the day -- well, Your Honour, am I allowed to respond or not? Because I see counsel getting -- Mr. Beneta at the end says, I don't know, but whether -- this is at page 46606-07, after a tonne of leading questions by counsel, but at the end of the day what Beneta says is: "... whether he actually read out this entire text, I don't know." That's the sum and substance -- let me finish my point. Let me finish my point. Now that's what it that's what it says. And we do disagree, and besides that, it's a false issue to say, well, it's only important if -- if the speech was given. That's again a characterisation we don't accept. Who says it was a speech not given? Who says? It's a document and it's signed and sealed by Mr. Petkovic. Look on the screen. Do you sign and seal outlines of speeches not given? Mr. Petkovic knew this was an important document. It was prepared as an important document. Whether it would be given orally, in writing or both, he signed and sealed it. We can't just simply blow -- dismiss it now and say, well, actually it's a text of a speech that was never given. The Prosecution doesn't accept that, and the only evidence that supports that position is the testimony of Mr. Petkovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm very glad that -- Your Honours. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you will have the floor, but let me tell you this: After scores of years working in a court, I was never faced -- I have never been faced with a situation when, in closing arguments, procedural matters are being broached. This is a sheer and a massive waste of time for everybody. You have the possibility to let him speak, finish. We'll draw our own consequences, and you will have your rejoinder, and you will be free to say then what you have to say. That's the adversarial system. Because if you are on your feet whenever he wants to speak to say we don't agree, we'll be here in another year. So what do you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to remind everybody that my colleagues before me spoke and intervened more often than I did, and you did not react the same way you did to my reaction, which I don't consider to be fair. Just because of what Mr. Scott said about the document, I would like this: I'm very glad that Mr. Scott provided such an explanation because this explanation clearly demonstrates that the burden of proof is on Defence in this trial and that my learned friend Mr. Scott says that in this specific case, the undelivered speech, for him, is a speech given until the moment when the Defence proves differently. My learned friend Mr. Scott did not provide a single document to prove that the speech was given, that Defence expected to prove differently, and this is what the factual burden is based on. There's no document to prove that the speech was given. I said in my final brief that I believe that the document does have relevance for the mens rea of General Petkovic, and the speech and all the pieces of evidence have been elaborated in my final brief, and if Mr. Scott needs to -- needed to say something else about that, he could have said it in the closing argument and not in the rebuttal. So we really should not allow Mr. Scott to abuse his time for -- to rebuttal and to reiterate the arguments that he should have presented in the earlier stages of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, so what was it that Mr. Filipovic may have said that would run counter to Ms. Alaburic's closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if I understand the -- the Chamber's question -- Mr. President's question correctly, it takes us back to an earlier point. Let me just give the Chamber -- excuse me while I go back to that point. If I can just give the Chamber the -- the critical citations and then the Chamber can of course -- what's most important is for the Chamber to decide its view of the evidence. I would ask the Chamber to consider in the context of the ABiH -- the Muslim members of the HVO, Mr. Filipovic's testimony at T 47643 to 44, again at 47649 to 50. On those -- on that point. If I've misunderstood Your Honour's question, I apologise, and perhaps you can assist me further as to that point. As to the so-called speech, and again that's a premise that we don't accept. That it was -- the reference there was to the witness Beneta, and that can be found at P -- at page 46606-07. And just -- I mean, again, read what Mr. Beneta says, and as much as counsel wants him to say that the speech wasn't given and the document not used, that's not what he says. That's not what he says. And when push came to shove, what he ultimately says is: "I don't know." But whether -- quote: "But whether he actually read out this entire text, I don't know." That's the sum and substance of Mr. Beneta's testimony on the point. Your Honour, if I can just be allowed to make then -- to wrap up our -- our final remarks and -- since I think I have the time to do so, I will afford myself the luxury of just making one additional record, comment, in light of the various things that have been said. Your Honour, I got up during the Defence closings and made an objection about the references to evidence not in the record, and to put it -- to put it colloquially, I was shouted down. I was told to sit down, that it wasn't appropriate to get up and to make objections, and I did. I sat down and I didn't -- I didn't get up again even though there were other opportunities or other reasons why I thought that I should have. Today the rules have been completely different. Today the rules have been completely different. I've been interrupted ad nauseam. We have tried to conduct this in good faith. We outlined our topics to the Chamber on Thursday. The Chamber consulted with each other. The Chamber ruled and gave us three hours. We prepared accordingly with what we understood was the scope. If I've been wrong on that, then I stand corrected, but there was none of this throughout the Defence closing arguments. There was none of this constant interruptions, constantly on our feet. We didn't do that. In fact, the one time I did do it, I was clearly told to sit down. And I think it's a bit unfortunate that the conduct today has been dramatically different. But if the Chamber will allow me to simply conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I would like to answer you on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think there is a fallacy in your sense of injustice, because there is a fundamental difference between final argument, the Prosecution, the Defence, and rebuttal. Rebuttal is -- is very subsidiary. It is rather exceptional, and it is supposed to be focused and not to be a continuation of -- of pleadings. That's the way this Chamber, following Judge Liu, has interpreted Rule 86(A). And here, of course, where you have a basic condition for the right to freedom of expression, as it were, there is a point where the other party can say you are overstepping the limits, whereas in the general pleadings there are no such limits, and therefore there's a different attitude. The Chamber is quite aware of the fact that it is different today. I must say, for one, I have anticipated this. It does not come as a surprise at all. I am sorry, probably there were misunderstandings in the sense at that we did not make it sufficiently clear how -- or to put it more precisely, that we approve and accept the points of the Defence's, mainly put I think by Mr. Khan, that the rebuttal should be limited in the way Judge Liu had pointed out. So I'm prepared to assume some responsibility for the frustration you feel, and it's regrettable, but our task is to see to it that the rules are respected. And the other parties' right is to ask for the rules to be respected. We certainly understand your feelings of frustration, but as I said before, probably such feelings are to be found on -- on all sides, and it is practically impossible to find a precise and all round convincing formula when you have six Defences and one Prosecutor on how much time to give these and that. You can discuss this endlessly. I don't think that you would come to a solution that would convince everyone. We have seen this throughout this trial. So I'm sorry if I have been perhaps a bit lengthy in these explanations, but I would hope that we did continue in a slightly relaxed -- more relaxed atmosphere until the end of these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to take the floor as well and to say the following: Within the Chamber we have, of course, spoken about this issue, and I did agree that certain restrictions should be applied on the Prosecution's rebuttal. My dissenting opinion is only about the following: I believe that Rule 86(A) in my view is rather clear and I quote: "After the presentation of all the evidence, the Prosecution may present a closing argument. Whether or not the Prosecutor does so, the Defence may make a closing argument." And now we come to the rebuttal, and I quote: "The Prosecutor may present a rebuttal argument to which the Defence may present a rejoinder." Now, in my view, Rule 86(A) doesn't speak about restrictions. I really very much in a way respect Judge Liu's position, but in my view, it is not a position which should be applied by all means and without any -- any regard to the necessities of this trial, and any trial, actually. And therefore, I am also -- I feel quite uneasy that the Prosecution could not and cannot continue and finish its rebuttal, although, of course, I also acknowledge that -- that on the decision of the Chamber, the -- our team has advised the Prosecution that it should take up those positions and arguments which have been included in the closing arguments -- rather, the Defence closing arguments. Now, I would like to -- in a way to close my remarks that -- that without a -- without listening to all the parties, I believe it would be a rather bad turn of events if we would then prevent anybody, let me say anybody, to speak up and to explain their positions. And, of course, I would also be very much in favour of the Defence teams to be heard and to be listened as far as their own comments and arguments are concerned. So it is what I wanted to say, but again, in my view, the very restrictive interpretation of Rule 86(A), it is not which I see it as a kind of final position of this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me add my voice to my Judges' opinions. I fully subscribe to Judge Trechsel's opinion. The Rules are very clear. After the Defence case, the Prosecutor -- the Prosecutor prepare -- will prepare their final brief, and the Defence will do the same, explaining and setting out all their arguments, which is different from civil law countries and systems where everything is said in court. But here, as per rules, everybody is allowed to express their arguments in writing. In a second stage of the proceedings, everybody, every party, is free to express their views in court; the Prosecution through their closing arguments, and the Defence through theirs. So everybody is supposed to be aware of the problems. But the Rules also provided for the possibility that there may be rebuttal, but, of course, the rebuttal to what was done before. As to the jurisprudence, the case law of this Tribunal, for instance through Judge Liu, it recalls that the rebuttal are to be limited, very restrictively, in order to avoid readdressing issues that have been dealt with before. And these are the circumstances under which Judge Trechsel and myself were of the view and decided that the Prosecutor was to address what had been said during the closing arguments in court. In such circumstances and facing such arguments that needed rebuttal, otherwise, there was no need for a rebuttal. I will remind you that we've conducting this trial for five years, and there must be an end to it eventually. So, Mr. Scott, you were about to end when Judge Trechsel spoke, and then the three Judges spoke. You have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All those things would be interesting for further discussion and perhaps at some future time there will be the opportunity to do that, but obviously it would not be productive to belabour them further now and what the proper -- what the jurisprudence is and what perhaps it should be. So we will leave it at that. If I might be allowed the courtesy of making just a few final observations, I would greatly appreciate that, just by way of summation, and it's going to take me maybe about three minutes if the Chamber and counsel might allow me to do that. Your Honour, I would just simply remind the Chamber in terms of the four important components that the Prosecution mentioned in the beginning of its closing arguments we feel are important guides to the analysis of this case, and those were the aspects of this case that this was a top-down project, the importance of territory, the importance of demographics, the importance of Croatness. The Herceg-Bosna behaviour charged in the indictment is simply too systematic -- is simply too systematic, too widespread, too consistent, too coordinated, too patterned and practiced over too long a period of time to have simply happened as random or isolated acts. It is too clearly tied together by high-level policy and strategy coming from Zagreb and Mostar to have simply happened as a series of random acts. In closing, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that, at the end of the day, there are two fundamental themes that run through the Defence cases, either explicitly or implicitly and I would add including during the closing arguments. The first of these is the denial of both knowledge and power. What Robert Jackson said at Nuremberg in July 1946 can just as appropriately be said today, that is: "To escape the implications of their positions and the inference of guilt from their activities, the defendants are almost unanimous in one defence. The refrain is heard time and again, these men were without authority, without knowledge, without influence, without importance. And to that would be added or concluded, and without responsibility." The Nuremberg accused Albert Speer, who was more forthright about the responsibility of the Nazi leadership than most of the others although an accused himself, referred to these denials when he talked about about the clear responsibility of the Nazi leadership of the top associates around Hitler with reference to utterly decisive matters there is total responsibility. Quote -- quoting now: "There must be total responsibility insofar as a person is one of the leaders because who else could assume responsibility for the development of events if not the immediate associates who work with and around the head of the state." Speer went further: "It is impossible after the catastrophe to evade the total responsibility. If the war had been won, the leaders would also have assumed total responsibility." There is a saying that captures what Speer said at Nuremberg: "Victory has a thousand fathers, but defeat is an orphan." I dare submit to the Chamber had things somehow gone differently and if Herceg-Bosna had somehow achieved something like independent statehood, none of these men would have declined to take full credit in the way that they now seek to avoid full responsibility. I return to Jackson again: "We seek to punish each for his own crime of joining a common criminal plan in which others also participated. The measure of the criminality of the plan and therefore of the guilt of each participant is, of course, the sum total of crimes committed by all in executing the plan, but the gist of the offence is participation in the formulation or execution of the plan. These are rules which every society has found necessary in order to reach men like these defendants who never get blood on their own hands, but who lay plans that result in the shedding of blood." These men in this dock on the face of this record were not strangers to this programme of crime, nor was their connection with it remote or obscure. We find them in the very heart of it. Your Honour, that's the Prosecution position in this case. We submit to you that the Prosecution has met its burden of proof. We ask the Chamber to find each of the six men guilty as charged. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break, because it's 20 past 12.00. We'll have a 20-minute break. I believe Mr. Karnavas wants to take the floor. Is that so?

utterances.text: Just to give an update to the Trial Chamber. I was provided with 15 minutes to rebut one point. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you properly, so there's 15 minutes you got last week, and you wish to address us for the rejoinder, and then we'll have Mr. Prlic speaking for some 15 minutes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That -- yes, that will be it. And I'll now try to be -- very quickly, it's going to be counter punching what the Prosecution brought up today, Your Honours. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And so how much time do you need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So whilst we are at it, what about the Stojic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we kindly ask you to present our position after the break. What Mr. Karnavas has just said is probably feasible during the day. We'll have to consult with our client whether he would like to take the floor and then make an assessment of the time necessary. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit, we would also like to make an evaluation. We don't want to be emotional but make a rational decision as to whether anything deserves a rejoinder or not. And we will also consult our client, but at any rate, we have no grand plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would also prefer to give you a more precise assessment of our -- of the time required after the break, after consulting General Petkovic. But what I can say for sure now is that we will ask for a rejoinder to what Mr. Stringer has said. He has spoken about our client for about 50 minutes, but my current assessment is that we will need about 30 [Realtime transcript read in error "15"] minutes for rejoinder to Mr. Stringer's word, and then we'll see what will happen afterwards in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will also consult my client but if Mr. Coric chooses to address the Trial Chamber, that, including our rejoinder, will not exceed half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your President. Unfortunately, I have nobody to consult because my client is not present so that he certainly will not address the Trial Chamber. We will need 5 minutes at the most to respond to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction of the record. I said that we will not need more than 30 minutes. "Fifteen" was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I wrote down. We're going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. We're going to go round once more since the Defence teams consulted with their respective clients over the break. Now, for the Prlic Defence, Mr. Karnavas told us already how much time he needed. As to the Stojic Defence, what was your decision?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Stojic Defence decided not to respond to the Prosecution's rebuttal. utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Praljak would like to take the opportunity given by you to address the Trial Chamber at the end, but he will only need a few minutes.
