utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 4D.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we stand by our request to get up to 30 minutes for rejoinder to the Prosecution. We wish to deal with legal issues. The Prosecution has offered some new interpretations, and we would like to respond to them. General Petkovic would also like to address the Trial Chamber at the end, and I support Ms. Nozica's suggestion that the accused speak after the rejoinders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 5D. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Coric does not wish to address the Trial Chamber, because he believes that all has been said by his Defence counsel already. As for the rejoinder, I will take very little time, and if I speak very slowly, I will need up to 30 minutes to respond to something Mr. Stringer dealt with. I mean two matters only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And finally Mr. Pusic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have spoken our mind a short time ago. We will need up to 10 minutes, and Mr. Pusic will not speak, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to discuss this and then we'll hand down a decision as to the time allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After deliberations, the Trial Chamber recalls that rejoinders fall under the same rules as those applying to rebuttals. Secondly, further to the Defence teams' requests, grants them. So over and above the 15 minutes given to the Prlic Defence for their rebuttal of another Defence team's arguments, we'll have 15 minutes to the rebuttal -- or rejoinder of the Prosecution's rebuttal, and Mr. Prlic will have 15 minutes for his address to the Judges. As for the Stojic Defence, there will be no intervention -- or no rejoinder, but there will be a 15-minute speech by Mr. Stojic. As to 3D, the Trial Chamber grants 10 minutes as part of the rejoinder and 15 minutes for Mr. Praljak's speech. 4D, 30 minutes are given to General Petkovic's Defence. Mr. Petkovic himself will have 15 minutes for his final words. With regard to the 5D team, the Trial Chamber grants 15 minutes to Mr. Coric's Defence and takes due note that Mr. Coric is not going to speak. Finally, regarding Mr. Pusic, the Trial Chamber grants five minutes to his team and notes that Mr. Pusic will not speak since he is absent from the courtroom. As a result, with regard to the time, the overall time, we will continue tomorrow for part of the day. But without further ado, Mr. Karnavas is going to start. It is five to 1.00, and we may proceed with him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. I will first begin by rebutting what I indicated last week, the one matter that came up with the Petkovic Defence and that has to do with the Ljubuski transit centres. The transcript pages -- the relevant transcript pages are 52558 to 52559. There are two particular points that I wish to draw out, and I will be making some reference to documents for your own consideration, Your Honours. The first is that the Petkovic Defence asserts that the purpose for the transit centres was for POWs. That's the first one that we categorically object to and we will be rebutting. The second point, of course, is that the Ljubuski transit centre was not supported by the -- the internationals, and we will rebut that as well. Now, the Petkovic Defence stated, and I quote: "Since military-able men of Muslim ethnicity were considered the reserve army of BH Army and hence they were prisoners of war, the initiative to establish a transit centre at Ljubuski was absolutely lawful and in line and keeping with the Third Geneva Convention, Article 12, paragraph 2." It is our contention and we believe the evidence supports that the Ljubuski centre was not set up for purposes of detaining POWs. It was set up for displaced persons from Central Bosnia, Croats, that is, as a result of the ABiH offensive. This was the only mission, we submit, for this particular transit centre. The record demonstrates a pressing -- at the time that there was a pressing need for such a centre given the huge influx of displaced persons coming from Central Bosnia and the fact that in Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna, there was little or no space available for them. And we refer to our final brief, paragraphs 202 to 219 where we've more fully developed our arguments. But in addition, we invite the Trial Chamber to look at P03394, which is a report on the work of the HZ-HB Office of Expelled Persons and Refugees for January to June 1993, where on page 3 it is stated, and I'm quoting part of the sentence: "The number of expelled Croats residing in HZ-HB has increased by 50.000, (i.e., 100 per cent) and now totals 110.061. It is likely that new expelled persons will be arriving in this area." We also draw Your Honours' attention to 1D00929, which is a letter from Zubak to Rebic sent on 23 July 1993. Zubak informed Rebic that there were approximately 8.000 expelled Croats, this -- 8.000 more, more, displaced Croats to arrive in Herzegovina from Central Bosnia, and he's pleading with Rebic, who was the counterpart of ODPR in the Republic of Croatia, and Zubak writes: "We believe, are aware, that we have almost exhausted our capacities for accommodating the displaced persons so that we cannot take care of newcomers. In that respect, you are kindly requested within the framework of your competencies to make efforts to allow us to relocate a part of displaced Croats from Kakanj and Konjic to facilities in the territory of the Republic of Croatia." We also invite the Trial Chamber's attention to P03796, and these are the minutes of the HVO HZ-HB meeting of the 48th session, dated 29 July 1993, where again in there there is -- it is recorded that Zubak had reported at this HVO meeting about the acceptance of 10.000 expelled Croats from Central Bosnia, and in the report, Zubak underlined two problems: One, the lack of accommodation capacities in the territory of HZ-HB; and two, insufficient number of vehicles necessary for evacuation of the population for the mentioned areas. So that's the one point that I wanted to draw to your attention regarding that. Then the Petkovic Defence indicated, and again it's referenced in those two pages which would have been on 21st February 2011, and I quote: "I think these are facts for which there is ample evidence in the case file." In other words, ample facts that the Ljubuski transit centre was set up for POWs. Well, the only evidence concerning this claim is the BA's 92 ter statement, which is P09712, and it's paragraph 50, which is rewritten in the OTP brief on paragraph 453, paragraph 41 and 42, rewritten -- 51, I'm sorry, 51 and 52, rewritten in the OTP brief 454 and paras 54 and 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I don't know if you're going to quote the evidence or not, but that can't be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was not. No, I was not. And that was rewritten in paras 455 in the OTP final brief. Now, when it comes to BA's testimony, I refer to my earlier comments. I can go on today in light of what we heard earlier about the credibility of these internationals, but I believe last week I indicated how BA's statement was compiled with the assistance of the OTP investigators, so I won't go into that. However, since there is the remark that there's ample evidence, I use this opportunity to -- and I believe it's within my right as part of the rejoinder or rebuttal, to point out that reports were inaccurate and sometimes outright misleading. And for an example, just as an example, if we look at P09847, and this is the international organisation which is reporting on 19 August 1993, to Zagreb office about alleged ethnic cleansing in western -- west Herzegovina, and I quote:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this is on page 2. But if you contrast that with, for instance, 1D01356, which is dated 20 October 1993, this gives an overview of the retired people in the local communities of Mostar municipality, and there we see that at that point in time there were approximately 2.000 -- 2.107 Muslim pensioners on the west side. And I also draw your attention with respect to this particular issue, BD's testimony where under -- when I cross-examined and I make reference to pages 20880 to 20883, where in particular I discuss 1D01356 and in particular where I -- I impeach her on her organisation's or her, in particular, use of humanitarian aid as a weapon. Then I also wish to draw to the Trial Chamber's attention 1D02813. This is a notebook from Marinko Simunovic. He was the head of the Red Cross of Mostar, and in his notebook dated 30 November 1993, based on a coordinating committee meeting that was held, and this was composed of all the humanitarian organisations, he reported, obviously it was done contemporaneously so he didn't know that it was done for the purposes of this trial, that at the time there were approximately 47.558 people in West Mostar, and of that, there were 9.928 Muslims, that is 20.84 per cent of the population, on West Mostar. So I -- and I'm mentioning this as a vignette. So when we're talking about the credibility of the reporting system, this is just one -- and I should point out the transcript pages, which are 33629 to 33638, and that was on 22 October 2008. And then the following day, on 23 October 2008, is 33673 to 3367 -- 76. We also wish to point out the testimony of Martin Raguz who came here, and then again this refutes this notion that there's ample evidence that the Ljubuski transit centre was for POWs. We take exception to that. Mr. Raguz was cross-examined rather aggressively and at length by the Prosecution, as is their right to do, and with respect to the Ljubuski transit centre, you can find the particular references to his testimony at pages 31522 to 31526. This would have been on 28 August 2008. And I specifically urge the Trial Chamber or draw your attention to 31525 to 31526. I'm prepared to quote from the transcript, but I think it is better to utilise our time by simply mentioning that he talked about what these transit centres were for, and it was his testimony that they were for the purposes of assisting those who wished to voluntarily lead -- leave, but they were of Croats from Central Bosnia that wanted to -- that had no place to go. Now, there are other -- the other point that I wanted to make with respect to this is that -- that there was no assistance from the part of the internationals, by the international organisations with respect to the establishment of the Ljubuski transit centre. And on page 52559, the Petkovic Defence stated: "I remind you that the Herceg-Bosna authorities contacted UNHCR and UNPROFOR for help in the establishment of the transit centre and the temporary transfer of prisoners of war to third countries. The UNHCR, upon consultation with their headquarters, concluded that they would thus contribute to ethnic cleansing and refuse to provide assistance after which UNPROFOR pulled out as well." We categorically refute this, and we draw your attention, Your Honours, to Mr. Raguz's testimony again, and this is on transcript page 31402 to 31405, testimony of 26 August 2008, and again on 31522 to 31526, 28 August 2008. And Mr. Raguz was rather explicit that it could not have been done without the assistance of the international humanitarian organisation. And lastly I point -- I draw your attention to P06324, page 3. This is part of a report of the activity of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and its ministries from November 1993 to March 1994, and it states: "Fortunately, in October 1993, Hotel Bistrica in Ljubuski, which had been and was being restored by international humanitarian organisations, was functioning as a reception centre where several thousand of displaced persons stayed for shorter or longer periods." So that -- that concludes my rebuttal with respect to this particular topic, Your Honours. And now very quickly, unless there are any questions, I will go through the Prosecution's rebuttal, and abiding by the rules, I will just go right through it. First, the Prosecution mentions that the Muslims -- that there was some sort of an objection by the Defence that the Muslims should not get to the sea. Well, you need to put this into context. No one has ever suggested that Neum was not part of Bosnia and Herzegovina or that the Muslims or the Serbs or the Croats should not have access to Neum. The whole point of getting to the sea had to do with in Croatia, and there, we submit, that the Muslims did not have a right to go into Croatia to try to occupy land for a deep-water port. In particular, they were looking towards Ploce. So we do take exception to the Prosecution's notion that somehow Halilovic, who was a Serbian Muslim, he was from Sandzak, or Ganic, again from Serbia, should have a right to Croatian territory. So when we talk about Muslims getting to the sea, that's what we're talking about. And there is ample evidence also in the Mladic diary, albeit part of it did not make it into the evidence. Croatian exceptionalism. I don't understand quite exactly what the Prosecution means by that. The Defence has endeavoured throughout this trial to be very clear on the evidence itself, and we -- at least the Prlic Defence has never advocated something for the Croats which it did not believe that the Muslims should also be entitled to. So we, too, take exception to that. As far as the single military command, there is no real issue here. The -- the Prlic Defence has never advocated that the ABiH was not a lawful armed force of BiH, but it wasn't the only one. There is a distinction between being an armed forces, which is what the friendship and co-operation agreement called for with ABiH and HVO being part of it, and I think we need to make that distinction. So when we're talking about the ABiH, we're talking about an army, one component of the armed forces. And as far as -- if you look at what happened in January 15, the purpose behind that, which was also something that had been discussed in -- in Geneva, was that in a region, in a particular region, it would be best for -- where you have two operating armies for there to be one in charge, and that was -- we -- we discussed this at length in our brief, so I'm not going to belabour the point, but our position was and remains that there was never an intolerance of the ABiH. It's just that in certain areas, because there was -- there was conflict, that it would be best to have one of the two armed -- armed forces, one of the two armies, take the lead and the other one being subordinated to it, which is why in areas where there was the Muslim majority provinces based on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, it had been agreed that the HVO would be subordinated to the ABiH. Moving on to Sarajevo and this top-down Muslim juggernaut. I don't understand this phraseology, I have to be honest. I think I understand what they're talking about. There's no mystery that as early as 1992, Mr. Owen says, and we brought this out already, that by 1992, Sarajevo -- the Sarajevo government was becoming more and more representative of only the Muslim ethnicity. The Serbs had walked away, but this -- these are his observations. Was Sarajevo cut off? It was. And we have to put it into context, Your Honour. You heard testimony, and I don't want to belabour the point, but you heard testimony from Primorac, for instance, who was there. You heard testimony also from one of our other witnesses who was 1DAA, Perkovic, Raguz. They all talked about how it was cut off, and for us in particular, our point was and remains is that the government could not function properly because the electrical grid was down, telecommunications didn't function. Now, they mentioned this software. Again, I invite your close scrutiny and attention to Mr. Tomic's testimony at the time, because I believe there was a comment even -- I believe it was from you, Judge Trechsel. The software had to do with the payment bureau system, the SDK, and he had indicated that it would have been much easier for them to have gone to Croatia to get a much more sophisticated software, but because they wanted to stay within the grid because it wasn't expected that the war would last forever, that it was to their advantage to have the software that was compatible with the rest of the country. So when you look at the context, somebody brings out the software, gives it to them. So when we're talking about cutting off, let's put matters in perspective. And also if they're going to be using Tomic for those purposes, consider what the purpose is behind getting the software. Impunity. I want to make sure that we're very, very clear after five years and I hope, I dare hope that I have never -- that we, the Prlic Defence, have never given the impression that we are for impunity. I think Dr. Prlic was very clear early on when he spoke, and I think that throughout our presentation while we have been rather vigorous in cross-examining witnesses, I do not believe that there's been a single incidents when we have subscribed to a culture of impunity, and nor did we try to represent matters in a way that crimes, however -- however minor they may be, should be overlooked. We tried to put matters into perspective. With regard to the JCE, I was to be, frankly, rather disturbed today. I would use the word "offended," but maybe that's a little too strong, but I was disturbed in the sense that the examples that were given were, first of all, are from other cases. They're trying to equate the Croats with the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Frankly, I don't believe that this is the place to have this sort of a discussion. This case rests on the facts and the facts alone. In our brief, we challenge, we challenge, the JCE, in particular JCE III. We maintain then as I maintain today and I will continue to maintain that JCE III was never a part of customary international law. Now it's up to Your Honours to decide whether it is or it isn't. But the whole argument on the JCE today, Your Honours, I would invite you to simply dismiss it outright. It has no place. You should decide this case based on the evidence that was presented before you, and I think making comparisons and saying oh, by the way, this other court, these other Judges, I think that's a soft way of trying to pressurise you into going into a particular direction. Not that I think it would work. With respect to Mr. Thornberry, well, you know, I never heard the saying before I heard it from Mr. Khan, but I did like it, you know, when you're jaundice everything looks yellow. I think probably there's a lot of meaning to that, and that's what exactly what I was trying to convey at the time. And we've already talked about the international witnesses. We simply invite you to look at their testimony in toto. Look at it together. And also ask yourselves, again ask yourselves if their memories are so solid, if they vividly recall all of these things, why is it that you have to sit down with somebody for four days and then work them over in a sense to come up with a draft and then another draft and then another draft. Show them documents that they haven't seen. So I do believe that the evidence is there for you, Your Honours, to make that determination as to how much weight, if any, to give to them. Now, they say, well, they got it right. The internationals could got it right. Well, I can point to a dozen of instances, but I go back to the one instance where you have Mr. Lane who says, well, Mr. Prlic had his own private restaurant because I went there, I'm in this room, a waiter comes in, and it's a private restaurant, and it turns out to be hotel restaurant service. How right can they get it if -- if that's the basis of their evidence? With respect to the borders, and they mention Akmadzic. First of all, I think -- and the testimony, I believe, was pages 29851 to 29852. Again, Your Honours, read the -- read those transcript pages very carefully before and after, of course, and I should -- of course there's no need for me to say this, but you will see that what Akmadzic is talking about is the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. We submit that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was never about borders. It was about areas. Now, the issue of borders came up -- come up in two contexts. One is the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. And who sets it up? It's the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That's when it started. So if they wanted to merge, why bother to have borders? Borders never existed, not even a sign, "Welcome to Croatia" or "Welcome to Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's number one. Number two and more importantly, the issue of borders really comes into play when we're talking about the provinces under the -- the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna -- the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. That's what we're talking about, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the provinces. And again, keep in mind that this is based on the international negotiations that are going on. It is not the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina driving the agenda. In fact, they're the only ones that keep signing whatever is brought to them, including the maps. So when we talk about borders, be very careful, Your Honours. Put things into context. With respect to Witness Ribicic. Yes, he was a 92 bis witness. I take that on board. However, keep in mind at the time that he prepared his report, he did not have the benefit of all of the presidential transcripts. Now, the Prosecutor would have you believe that he did an honest intellectual report. I say rubbish. It was not. A constitutional analysis does not refer to a presidential transcript from 27 December 1991, based on what Tudjman might have said before the establishment of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and say, Based on this, I can conclude that this was the purpose. An honest, objective report would have been for the gentlemen to strictly look at the founding documents, look at the constitution of BiH, maybe have some sort of a historical background, do something to the -- similar to what our Witness Cvikl did, but this was not done by Mr. Rebic. In fact, he was relying on things -- Ribicic, I'm sorry. He was relying on such things as what he read in the newspaper. And when the new material came out, when the new presidential transcripts came out, and there was even an exchange, I vividly recall this, with you, Judge Trechsel, because you said well, he doesn't have to read everything, and I understand -- and reading it in context I understand where you were coming from, but my point is this: If new material comes out that is relevant to the study that you just did, I think it behooves you to at least look at it. And when circumstances change, opinions may change with those circumstances as well, and I think it's -- so that's our criticism of Ribicic. Our criticism of Tomljanovich, you know it. I don't have to go through it. I think it's rather clear. With respect to Pellnas, the only thing that I wish to point out regarding Pellnas is that you can take a look at his entire testimony. Look at his demeanour. Look at the way he characterised individuals. And regrettably, regrettably, portions of the Mladic diary did not come in because we see a dark character, someone who certainly was playing one side against the other, and I'm particularly referring to the one conversation that he's having with Mladic in Mount Jahorina. So -- and if I may take this opportunity, since the Prosecution is calling him a true professional, I think that the Trial Chamber is perfectly capable to exercise its own judicial discretion and to revisit the issue to determine whether what was in the Mladic diaries concerning Pellnas should be admitted. It's never too late. Regarding the Croat moderate witnesses. Yes, we heard -- we heard Kljuic, and Kljuic has some baggage. First of all, he confabulated in a sense when he called himself a dissident. Everybody laughed at that notion. What's important about -- about Kljuic is he leaves the Presidency and then at some point he gets reappointed when clearly the rules did not provide for that. But aside from -- aside from him and if you do read Kljuic, I invite your close scrutiny and attention to the four or five or six hours that I cross-examined him because through his -- through that cross-examination you get a pretty good flavour of the circumstances at the time. But then they mention Brkic, Pelivan and Markesic. Who are -- where -- did these individuals come and testify? Were they subjected to cross-examination? The answer is no. So when they say Brkic was a moderate, how so? Based on what? Now, with respect to the legitimacy of the Presidency, in particular Izetbegovic. They want you to look at Akmadzic, and you know what, Your Honours? I say please do. I vividly recall -- I don't have the transcript page -- no, actually, I do have the transcript page where you should look at, because Akmadzic was on direct examination. We're talking about Izetbegovic being elected the first time, being re-elected the second time, and then his term was about to expire and he had to have a trip to go to Geneva. And Akmadzic says to him, "Mr. President, you know, you're going to have to resign, you know, so we need to have, you know, elections for the new next president." And he says, well, afterwards we'll do it. And then it's pointed out again, but it's going to be expired, you're going to be out of the country. At which point Izetbegovic says, "I'll talk to Tudjman." Now, one of the -- you could be looking at, Your Honours, are 1D02940. Look at 18 June 2008, pages 29514 through to 29517. And also while you're at it, because it might be helpful, look at the constitution of the Social Republic of BiH, Article 358 at 1D02994. And it would not hurt also to look at the Presidency Rule of Procedure Article 19, P10509. But let's go back to this. What does Tudjman have to do with the Presidency of BiH? How legitimate can the government be? Let's assume, let's assume that -- that what was said by -- by Okun, that, well, you know, it was recommended by Izetbegovic to Boban. How legitimate can that Presidency be? In what sense? And so our position was and remains that Izetbegovic was lawfully elected to that position as president for the first time. He was lawfully elected the second time. Beyond that, he had a responsibility to step down, and he did not. And Lord Owen, as he indicated, treated the -- the Presidency at some point became representative of basically just the Muslim nation. So for the Prosecution now to say, well, Tudjman arranged it with Boban, that's utterly ridiculous. How does that make the Sarajevo government a lawful Presidency? It does not. I wonder in which one of our countries we could do that where some other -- you know. Imagine the Canadian president saying, well, we'll do this for the United States. It doesn't make any sense. This is not our war. You know, the context of this statement we've discussed, but again they bring it up today. And you have to think back. Why is this phrase so important? It is important because of the perception, that's why. It is the perception of those who were not part of Izetbegovic's inner circle or of his nation. Witness 1DAA. You heard his testimony. He was on the stand approximately seven days, as I recall, maybe even eight. All I can say is take -- rather than cherry pick one particular phrase, you need to look at his entire testimony as a whole. There is a great deal there with respect to that one issue. It wasn't just one page. So I suggest, Your Honours, that rather that just look at the one phrase that the Prosecution points out, look at the entire -- his entire testimony. The third term I've already talked about. The third term -- Izetbegovic did not deserve a third term, could not have received a third term lawfully under the law at the time, and I think it's -- it's improper now to suggest that Izetbegovic could have. The -- with respect to the HVO being the only armed forces in 1992, in the spring of 1992. The Prlic Defence has never submitted that they were the only armed forces. You had the Patriotic League and you had the Green Berets. They organised themselves separately. They were the Muslim armed forces that belonged to the SDA party and they organised themselves clandestinely. At some point, the Croats of BiH and the Muslims of BiH took on what was perceived as their -- their common enemy, and we've heard plenty of testimony on that. With respect to the Stojic proclamation, I think I will rest on our brief. It's all covered there. Nothing is new. Finally, just let me -- and by saying that the final remarks by the Prosecution were not rebuttal at all, it was another closing argument, and invoking Albert Speer, I found again to be rather disturbing. First, he's a disturbing character throughout that ordeal, and what he says is virtually irrelevant. Self-serving, I would say. But I do want to point out since they're bringing Albert Speer and they're saying if the war would have gone differently, the bottom line is this, Your Honours, Dr. Jadranko Prlic was part of the Washington -- when the Washington Agreement came in was part of the federation government and part of the ABiH government. He was put in a position that was highly responsible which was minister of the defence while the war was still raging, and after Dayton, he continues to be with the same government, having a very responsible position as the minister of foreign affairs. And I'll leave at that, Your Honours. And I think any comparison between the Nazis and the Croats are inappropriate in this courtroom. I believe I have covered all the points I wanted, Your Honour, and unless there are any questions, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. It will soon be time to stop, so I think it's best that we continue tomorrow. Therefore, tomorrow we will hear D3, D4, D5, and D6. So we should -- before the first break we will be done with the rejoinders. Then after the break, each accused willing to take the floor will have this opportunity. Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the Prlic Defence had a chance to rebut some of our closing arguments, I kindly ask you up to five minutes for rejoinder to their rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me consult my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber deliberated, and we'll grant you five additional minutes, which means that altogether tomorrow you will have 35 minutes. I wish you all a good afternoon. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
